title: Session 5: Population Structure
text:
Yesterday afternoon you measured variation on your scaffold and compared two populations with it. Today we ask a different question, and we stop assuming we know who the populations are. Given only the genotypes, how do these individuals group together?
Two complementary methods answer that. A PCA makes no assumptions about populations at all and simply asks which individuals resemble each other. sNMF fits an explicit model in which each individual draws its ancestry from some number of genetic clusters. When the two agree, you have something. When they disagree, you have something more interesting.






NotePlan for the session




Finish plotting the statistics from yesterday — π, Tajima’s D and Fst along your scaffold
Run a PCA on the genotypes and plot it
Run sNMF, choose a value of K, and make an admixture plot
Put the two side by side and decide what they are telling you, and what they are not

The morning is for getting the analyses to run. The afternoon is for interpretation, and for the group discussion of what the whole room has found.








Note

TipYesterday’s plots first



Before starting anything new, finish the plots from Session 4: nucleotide diversity, Tajima’s D and Fst along your scaffold, with the position on the x axis.
Plot them one above the other on a shared axis. A region that stands out in all three is the thing you spent yesterday looking for, and it is much easier to see in aligned panels than in three separate figures. Remember to plot the number of variants per window as well, so you can tell a real feature from an empty window.

title: Session 5: Population Structure
text:
PCA
Replace underscores with nothing
VCF=your_scaffold_filtered.vcf
sed "s/_//g" "$VCF" > "${VCF%.vcf}_renamed.vcf"
Run PCA generation through plink
plink --vcf "${VCF%.vcf}_renamed.vcf" --allow-extra-chr --pca






NoteWhy the underscores have to go, and a shell trap in the original





PLINK reads a VCF’s sample names into a .fam file with two identifier columns, a family ID and an individual ID, and it splits names containing an underscore between the two. Watch what it does to our naming convention:
sample in VCF      FID     IID
Bil_01       ->    Bil     01
Her_03       ->    Her     03
The sample is now called 01, in a family called Bil. Every downstream step that matches on the individual name then fails or, worse, silently matches the wrong thing. Stripping the underscores first keeps each name whole, so Bil01 appears as both the family and the individual ID — which is exactly what the R code below depends on when it reads column V1 and calls it ID.
There is a cleaner, more surgical alternative worth knowing:
plink --vcf "$VCF" --allow-extra-chr --double-id --pca
--double-id tells PLINK to use the whole sample name for both ID columns and not split on the underscore at all, which leaves your VCF untouched.
The shell trap. The original form of the first command was:
sed "s/_//g" $VCF > $VCF_renamed.vcf
In bash, $VCF_renamed is not “the variable VCF followed by the text _renamed” — it is a different variable, named VCF_renamed, which does not exist. It expands to nothing, so the command writes to a file called .vcf and your real output never appears. Underscores are legal in variable names, which is precisely why this fails silently. If you want to append text to a variable, brace it: ${VCF}_renamed.vcf.
Also note what the sed affects: it removes every underscore in the whole file, including from chromosome and scaffold names. If your scaffold is called scaffold_12 it is now scaffold12, which matters when you cross-reference positions against the GFF3.









Tip



plink v1.9 is a lot better and more reliable than plink v2. Always check which version of your software is best suited to your needs!








NoteWhat --allow-extra-chr is for, and the warning you will see





PLINK was written for human data and expects chromosomes named 1–22, X, Y and MT. A scaffold name from a fungal assembly is none of those, and without --allow-extra-chr PLINK stops rather than guessing. This is the same human-centric assumption we met in the pipeline on Tuesday, in a different tool.
You will also probably see a warning recommending a minor allele frequency filter. Take it seriously: a PCA is strongly influenced by rare variants, and singletons — variants seen in exactly one individual — can pull that individual away from everyone else and produce a component that describes nothing but sequencing noise. Try the PCA with and without --maf, and see whether your conclusions survive.



#PCA
pca_eigenval = read.table("teaching/forest_popgen/plink.eigenval", header = F, sep = " ")
pca_eigenvec = read.delim("teaching/forest_popgen/plink.eigenvec", header = F, sep = " ")

names(pca_eigenvec)[names(pca_eigenvec) == 'V1'] <- 'ID'
pca_eigenvec = pca_eigenvec %>%
  mutate(Population = case_when(
    startsWith(ID, "BIL") ~ "bil",
    startsWith(ID, "BNP") ~ "bnp",
    startsWith(ID, "Her") ~ "her",
    startsWith(ID, "Iss") ~ "iss",
    startsWith(ID, "Kai") ~ "kai",
    startsWith(ID, "Koi") ~ "koi",
    startsWith(ID, "Kot") ~ "kot",
    startsWith(ID, "Luu") ~ "luu",
    startsWith(ID, "Met") ~ "met",
    startsWith(ID, "Mor") ~ "mor",
    startsWith(ID, "Mus") ~ "mus",
    startsWith(ID, "Myl") ~ "myl",
    startsWith(ID, "Pam") ~ "pam",
    startsWith(ID, "Pat") ~ "pat",
    startsWith(ID, "Pet") ~ "pet",
    startsWith(ID, "Puk") ~ "puk",
    startsWith(ID, "Rus") ~ "rus",
    startsWith(ID, "Sig") ~ "sig",
    startsWith(ID, "Skj") ~ "skj",
    startsWith(ID, "eSK") ~ "skj",
    startsWith(ID, "Spk") ~ "spk",
    startsWith(ID, "Sus") ~ "sus",
    startsWith(ID, "Ulv") ~ "ulv",
    startsWith(ID, "Van") ~ "van",
    startsWith(ID, "Ves") ~ "ves"))

pca_eigenvec = pca_eigenvec %>%
  mutate(Location = case_when(
    startsWith(ID, "BIL") ~ "Sweden",
    startsWith(ID, "BNP") ~ "Poland",
    startsWith(ID, "Her") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Iss") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Kai") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Koi") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Kot") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Luu") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Met") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Mor") ~ "Norway",
    startsWith(ID, "Mus") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Myl") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Pam") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Pat") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Pet") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Puk") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Rus") ~ "Russia",
    startsWith(ID, "Sig") ~ "Norway",
    startsWith(ID, "Skj") ~ "Norway",
    startsWith(ID, "eSK") ~ "Norway",
    startsWith(ID, "Spk") ~ "Norway",
    startsWith(ID, "Sus") ~ "SWF",
    startsWith(ID, "Ulv") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Van") ~ "NEF",
    startsWith(ID, "Ves") ~ "SWF"
  ))

row_id <- seq(1, nrow(pca_eigenval))
pca_eigenval$row_id = row_id

#Plot eigenval 
ggplot(pca_eigenval, aes(x = row_id, y = V1)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

#Plot eigenved
ggplot(pca_eigenvec, aes(x= V4, y= V3, col = Population)) +
  geom_point()






NoteWhich column is which





--pca writes two files, and knowing their layout saves a lot of confusion:







File
Contents




plink.eigenval
One row per component, holding its eigenvalue


plink.eigenvec
One row per individual: family ID, individual ID, then one column per component



So in plink.eigenvec, read as a headerless table:



Column
Holds




V1
Family ID — the sample name, once the underscores are gone


V2
Individual ID — the same name again


V3
PC1


V4
PC2


V5
PC3


V6
PC4



The plot in the code above therefore puts PC2 on the x axis and PC1 on the y. For the other pairs you were asked for, PC2 against PC3 is V4 and V5, and PC3 against PC4 is V5 and V6.
Two notes on the code as written. The file paths are from my machine, so change them to yours. And a PCA has no inherent orientation — the sign of a component is arbitrary, so your plot may be a mirror image of your neighbour’s even when the analysis is identical. That is not a mistake, and it is a good reason never to describe a result as “on the left”.









NoteWhat a PCA of genotypes is actually doing





Each individual is a long vector of genotypes. A PCA finds the directions in that high-dimensional space along which individuals differ most, and gives you each individual’s position along those directions. No population labels go in; any grouping you see in the output came out of the genotypes themselves.
That is its strength and its limitation.
The eigenvalues matter. Each eigenvalue is the amount of variance its component explains, which is why you were asked to plot them. If PC1 explains a few per cent more than PC2 and the rest trail off evenly, no component is capturing a strong structure, and reading a story into the scatter plot is over-interpretation. Plotting the eigenvalues first is what stops you doing that.
Distance in a PCA is not a tree, and clusters are not populations. Individuals close together are genetically similar, which can mean shared ancestry, but can equally mean similar amounts of missing data, similar sequencing depth, or similar rates of relatedness. More subtly, a continuous gradient of ancestry across geography — isolation by distance — also produces smooth, structured PCA axes, and those can look convincingly like discrete clusters when you only have a sample of individuals.
So before concluding anything: colour your PCA by sequencing depth and by missingness as well as by population. If PC1 correlates with depth rather than with geography, PC1 is a technical artefact and you have just saved yourself an embarrassing conclusion.

text:
LD (We are not going to do this in the course today)
Use scaffolds where _ are removed. This step is usually very memory intensive, so splitting the dataset into scaffolds is usually necessary. Under normal assumptions you would not expect unique chromosomes to be linked
plink --vcf $VCF_renamed.vcf --allow-extra-chr --out plink-test --r2 --ld-window-r2 0 --ld-window 0 --ld-window-kb 8000 
#from https://www.biostars.org/p/300381/
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

dfr <-read.delim("in_file",sep="",header=F,check.names=F,stringsAsFactors=F)
colnames(dfr) <- c("dist","rsq")
dfr$distc <- cut(dfr$dist,breaks=seq(from=min(dfr$dist)-1,to=max(dfr$dist)+1,by=10000))
dfr1 <- dfr %>% group_by(distc) %>% summarise(mean=mean(rsq),median=median(rsq))
dfr1 <- dfr1 %>% mutate(start=as.integer(str_extract(str_replace_all(distc,"[\\(\\)\\[\\]]",""),"^[0-9-e+.]+")),

end=as.integer(str_extract(str_replace_all(distc,"[\\(\\)\\[\\]]",""),"[0-9-e+.]+$")),
mid=start+((end-start)/2))

#Plot
ggplot(dfr1, aes(x=start,y=mean))+
    geom_line()






NoteWhat this would tell you, if we had time





Linkage disequilibrium is the association between alleles at different positions. Two variants that are inherited together more often than chance are in LD, and because recombination breaks those associations up over time, LD decays with physical distance along a chromosome. The code above bins pairs of variants by the distance between them and plots mean r² against that distance.
The shape of that decay is informative in itself. LD that decays within a few kilobases indicates frequent recombination, which in a fungus means regular sexual reproduction and outcrossing. LD that stays high over long distances indicates the opposite: clonal or highly selfing reproduction, where whole haplotypes are passed on intact.
That is the question yesterday’s Hardy–Weinberg test could not answer for a haploid organism. LD decay is one of the ways you can ask it. If you want something to do after the course, this is the analysis to come back to.

title: Session 5: Population Structure
text:
Population Structure
There are many ways to determine population structure. We will use sNMF.
Convert the VCF to a .geno file with LEA in R. Here is some example code
library(LEA)
library(tidyverse)
# Creation of a file called "example.vcf"
# with 4 SNPs for 3 individuals.
data("example_vcf")
write.table(example_vcf,"example.vcf",col.names =
    c("#CHROM", "POS", "ID", "REF", "ALT", "QUAL", "FILTER", "INFO",
    "FORMAT", "SAMPLE0", "SAMPLE1", "SAMPLE2"),
    row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

# Conversion    from the vcf format ("example.vcf") 
#               to the geno format ("example.geno").
# By default,   the name of the output file is the same name
#               as the input file with a .geno extension.
# Create files: "example.geno",
#               "example.vcfsnp" - SNP informations,
#               "example.removed" - removed lines. 
output = vcf2geno("example.vcf")

# Conversion    from the vcf format ("example.vcf")
#               to the geno format with the output file called "plop.geno".
# Create files: "plop.geno",
#               "plop.vcfsnp" - SNP informations,
#               "plop.removed" - removed lines. 
output = vcf2geno("example.vcf", "plop.geno")

# As force = false and the file "example.geno" already exists,
# nothing happens.
output = vcf2geno("example.vcf", force = FALSE)
The converted file can be used by sNMF to create the admixture plots
library(LEA)
library(tidyverse)
### Example of analysis using snmf ###
# Creation of the genotype file: genotypes.geno.
# The data contain 400 SNPs for 50 individuals.
#data("tutorial")
#write.geno(tutorial.R, "genotypes.geno")
################
# running snmf #
################
project.snmf = snmf("yourfiles.GT.FORMAT.geno",
K = 1:20,
entropy = TRUE,
ploidy = 1,
repetitions = 10,
project = "new")
# plot cross-entropy criterion of all runs of the project
plot(project.snmf, cex = 1.2, col = "lightblue", pch = 19)
# get the cross-entropy of the 10 runs for K = 4
ce = cross.entropy(project.snmf, K = 4)
# select the run with the lowest cross-entropy for K = 4
best = which.min(ce)
#add names
metadata = read.table("your .d file", header =T)
indv_snmf = read_tsv("your isolate name filet", col_names = F)
names(indv_snmf) = "Sample"
datalist = list()
for (i in c(6, 7, 8, 9)){
best = which.min(cross.entropy(project.snmf, K = i))
temp = as.data.frame(Q(project.snmf, i, best))
temp= cbind(indv_snmf, temp)
temp = temp %>%
gather("Cluster", "Admix_coef", -"Sample") %>%
mutate(K=i)
datalist[[i]] = as.tibble(temp)
}
snmf_results_per_K = bind_rows(datalist)%>%
inner_join(., metadata, by = c("Sample" = "Isolate")) %>%
unite(ID, Country, Location, Host, col = "for_display", remove = F)
ggplot(snmf_results_per_K, aes(x = reorder(Sample, ID), y = Admix_coef, fill = Cluster,
text = for_display)) +
geom_bar(position = "stack", stat = "identity", show.legend = F) +
facet_grid(K~.) +
theme_bw() +
theme(axis.title = element_blank(),
axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1),
legend.title = element_blank())
# display the Q-matrix
#my.colors <- c("tomato", "lightblue",
#"olivedrab", "gold")
#barchart(project.snmf, K = 4, run = best,
#border = NA, space = 0, col = my.colors,
#xlab = "Individuals", ylab = "Ancestry proportions",
#main = "Ancestry matrix") -> bp
#axis(1, at = 1:length(bp$order),
#labels = bp$order, las = 3, cex.axis = .4)






Importantploidy = 1



Note that argument in the snmf() call. It is the most important line in the block, and the whole reason we have been careful about ploidy all week: sNMF has to know that each individual carries one allele per locus, not two. Leave it at the default and the model is wrong for this organism, and it will not tell you so — it will return ancestry coefficients that look entirely plausible.








WarningRun this on the cluster



K = 1:20 with repetitions = 10 is 200 separate runs of the algorithm. On a real dataset that is not a thing to run in an interactive R session while twenty other people are doing the same on the same login node.
Put it in a batch script, as you learned on Tuesday, and submit it. While it runs, plot your PCA. If you want results sooner, narrow the range of K — there is rarely a reason to test twenty clusters for twenty-five populations’ worth of individuals, and you can always extend the range afterwards.








NoteChoosing K, and what the admixture plot does and does not show





sNMF estimates, for each individual, the proportion of its genome attributable to each of K ancestral genetic clusters. You choose K. The cross-entropy criterion — the thing plotted by plot(project.snmf, ...) in the code above — helps, by measuring how well each K predicts genotypes that were masked during fitting. Lower is better, and the usual advice is to take the K at which the curve levels off.
Be careful how much weight you put on that.
K is a parameter of the model, not a property of nature. There is no true number of populations waiting to be found. Different values of K are different resolutions at which to describe the same data, and several may be worth showing — which is exactly why the code loops over K = 6 to 9 and facets the plot, rather than reporting one number.
The clusters have no names and no history. sNMF gives you cluster 1, 2, 3. It does not tell you that cluster 1 is “the Finnish population” — you infer that by looking at which individuals carry it, using metadata that the model never saw. Keep the inference and the output separate in your writing.
Mixed ancestry is not proof of admixture. An individual shown as half one cluster and half another is consistent with recent mixing between two populations, but it is equally consistent with being from an unsampled population intermediate between the two, or from a continuous gradient that K clusters cannot represent. Structure plots are routinely over-read on exactly this point in the published literature.
Run it more than once. The algorithm starts from a random position and can settle in different places, which is why the code requests ten repetitions and selects the run with the lowest cross-entropy. If repeated runs at the same K give substantially different answers, that instability is itself a result, and reporting only the prettiest run is not honest.









TipThe kai question



Yesterday you were told that the authors did not report a location for the kai population, and that it had been assigned to north-eastern Finland. You now have two independent ways of checking that, neither of which uses the assignment itself:

In the PCA, do the kai individuals sit among the other NEF populations, or somewhere else?
In the sNMF output, do they carry the same ancestry proportions as the NEF populations?

If both say NEF, the guess was good. If they disagree with each other, think about why two methods on the same genotypes might reach different answers — that is a more interesting outcome than either verdict.








NoteDiscussion




How much variance do your first few principal components explain? Is there a strong structure in these data at all?
Does your PCA correlate with anything technical — depth, missingness, the scaffold you were assigned?
Which K does the cross-entropy curve favour? How different do the admixture plots look either side of it?
Do the PCA and the sNMF plot tell the same story? Where exactly do they disagree?
Yesterday’s Fst between your populations was presumably low. Is that consistent with what you see today?
The paper reports high gene flow. Having now seen the structure yourself, what in your output supports that, and what would you want before you believed it?
Each group analysed a different scaffold. Should structure estimated from one scaffold agree between groups? What would it mean if it did not?

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
text:
Caution



While the lure of AI is becoming more present in our daily lives, remember that you do not need it. You were perfectly able to design a packing list for your upcoming trip. You were able to look at a paper to find answers to your scientific questions. You knew how to query a vignette in R to determine how a function could be implemented.
Life was a bit slower, but you used your mind and your agency. You made decisions. Please do not confuse convenience with need!

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
text:
Introduction
In the past 3 years, AI has become more mainstream. The primary kind of AI people think of, is a Large Language Model (LLM). At this point, you cannot really avoid contact with these models anymore as they have infiltrated every aspect of the internet.



Searching LLM with Google to be answered with an LLM response


These algorithms are language models trained on incredibly large datasets. They are trained to recognise and generate natural language. The chatbots we are all familiar with are generative pretrained transformers (GPTs). These can be trained for specific tasks, or guided by prompt generation.
This is not an AI theory course, and we really do not have enough knowledge to explain the underlying theory beyond a rudimentary level. We would like to discuss the impact of AI on you as a user, and advocate for responsible use of AI in your current and future work.

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
text:
Machine Learning in Bioinformatics
Machine learning (ML) has been used in bioinformatics and other fields of data science for many decades on every level. Before ML, algorithms had to be programmed by hand rather than having the algorithms learn features of a dataset. With ML, features of a dataset can be annotated based on previously annotated datasets. These algorithms were a mix of supervised (learning on annotated data) and unsupervised (learning on unannotated data) learning, depending on the function of the algorithm.
Supervised algorithms are used for classification and regression analyses. Unsupervised algorithms are used to discover hidden patterns in data without needing a human’s input. Unsupervised algorithms are used in clustering, association, and dimensionality reduction






Note





Classification: Output is a discrete variable. Linear classifiers, support vector machines, decision trees, random forests. E.g. annotating a new genome based on genome annotations from existing species.
Regression: Focus on understanding dependent and indepedent variables



For more info, see here, and here.
There is no arguing that these algorithms have led to great progress within the field of bioinformatics. Generative AI is one of the next steps in the evolution of applying machine learning in our lives.

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
section: Incorporation of AI in Our Lives
text:
Incorporation of AI in Our Lives
ChatGPT gained 100 million users in the 2 months after its release in 2022, making it the fastest-growing consumr application in history. Generative AI (GenAI) models now come in many different flavours, depending on the developer.



GenAI chatbots by market share in August 2025 from FirstPageSage


As with earlier iterations of supervised and unsupervised algorithms, these self-supervised algorithms also need data to be trained.

Training Data
GenAI has all been trained on existing data. There has always been a bias in whose information gets captured. In a historical context, history was recorded by the party that won the war and destroyed existing knowledge. This also changed as different empires and narratives rose and fell. With digitisation, this information has landed on the internet. In the more modern “Internet Age”, everyone with an internet connection can technically post anything they’d like on the internet. There are different biases at play- not everyone has equal access to the internet, some people may not have strong enough opinions to post about something online, some people prefer to read rather than contribute, while others take pleasure in “shit-posting”.
The differences in how people use the internet have an effect on how useful the trained models become. In this example, you can clearly see what the effect of bad training data is.



GenAI answer to a simple question


GenAI’s are not programmed to say that they do not know something, and will happily hallucinate an answer. If you do not know better, or trust the computers, you may take this answer as true and post it elsewhere. As the use of AI’s increases, AI generated content is used to train new AI’s. Gary Illyes from Google has spoken about “human curated” vs “human created” data being used as training data.
In a perfect world, GenAI would be trained on perfectly curated data, but even with all of the data that we have on the internet at the moment, we do not have nearly enough data for this. We have to make do with what we have.

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
text:
Some Words of Caution
GenAI is becoming more integrated in every sector of our lives. It is important that we use the new technology responsibly. When Google first came out, there were classes on how to use the search engine, determine validity of sources and information, and how to stay safe on the internet. This section aims to raise awareness about commonly overlooked aspects of GPT use.

Learning with AI
AI has great potential in the field of education. ChatGPT has been shown to be highly beneficial in an educational environment when integrated properly. However, the use of AI in this setting must be balanced and carefully curated. A 2025 pre-print by Kosmyna et al showed that adults that used ChatGPT to write SAT type essays were outperformed consistently by adults that wrote the same essay without the support of an AI, and had significantly lower brain engagement.


Productivity with AI
A recent study by a non-profit group, Model Evaluation and Threat Research [(METR)https://metr.org/] aimed to quantify the difference in productivity when using AI. Participants in this study were not new to their field, with at least 5 years of experience prior to this study being conducted.



AI reducing productivity


The study also found that when AI is allowed, the participants spent less time coding and seeking solutions to the problems. Rather, they spent time prompting the AI, reading and reviewing responses, and being idle. Intel produced similar findings.



Reasons for loss of productivity with AI


If one combines the effect of passively learning with AI and the loss of productivity with, it becomes clear that AI must be used very carefully.


Data Privacy and Legal Concerns
Data privacy has been vital in the development and use of AI. The use of copyrighted material in training AI is being discussed and debated in several courts. The questions around using text and data mining are divisive with some parties arguing that finding patterns, trends, and insights in existing data being how new research is done by humans and should be extended to AI, while others, particularly in the European context, disagree to some extent. Understanding the legality of the service you use in different countries falls on you as a user.
The Terms of Service (ToS) of different GPTs are important when deciding whether to use a GPT at all. For example, Deepseek’s ToS (collected on 15.08.2025) states
Account Personal Data. We collect Personal Data that you provide when you set up an account, such as your date of birth (where applicable), username (where applicable), email address and/or telephone number, and password.
User Input. When you use our Services, we may collect your text input, prompt, uploaded files, feedback, chat history, or other content that you provide to our model and Services (“Prompts” or "Inputs"). We generate responses (“Outputs”) based on your Inputs.
Personal Data When You Contact Us. When you contact us, we collect the Personal Data you send us, such as proof of identity or age, contact details, feedback or inquiries about your use of the Services or Personal Data about possible violations of our Terms of Service (our “Terms”) or other policies.
Biological data enjoys a high level of protection, and is often considered as highly sensitive. Too often, users will input sequences, tables, or other data into a GPT to find ways to plot data, perform sequence annotations, or similar tasks. Be wary of doing this. Check the ToS explicitly, and frequently. Try to use GDPR compliant GPT’s if you must use a GPT.
AI as browser extensions steal deeply personal information when enabled in a users’ browser including financial, education, and medical information, whether an extension is being actively used or not. The authors have also commented on how these practices interfere with the company’s own ToS as well as privacy legislation.


Personal Responsibility
You as a user are responsible for the AI generated content you choose to use. If you, for instance, ask AI to generate a brand logo for you that is too close to something that exists already, the original owner is free to sue you as an individual for copyright infringement.
As scientists, we know that we should use peer-reviewed resources whenever possible. It is why we cannot cite Wikipedia in a scientific article. GPT’s have been widely shown to fabricate citations based on how it has learnt a citation should look. It is up to you as a user to check every single citation that AI generates since you are responsible for what you write.


Global Linguistic Changes
Even though ChatGPT has only been widely used for 3 years, it has already started leaving its traces in how we speak. Words like delve and meticulous are being used more frequently in academic YouTube talks.



GPT words in YouTube videos from Yakura et al 2025


It has also been shown that different GPT’s have different writing styles, also known as idiolects.
Some projects like this one are trying to match GPT ideolects match that of unique users. This will make detecting AI use more difficult in future.






This course was written by two people, and each person wrote their own sections without the use of any AI. Can you tell who wrote which sections based on idiolects?



We know that subtle linguistic shifts can change emotional regulation within an individual. We also know that sociolinguistics, even the slightest linguistic features, serve to bind or divide us.


AI on the Internet
Social media platforms are an important aspect in the development, improvement, and implementation of GenAI models. OpenAI, the creators of ChatGPT, have used a subreddit on the social media platform, Reddit, to train their new algorithm. Google and OpenAI have contractual agreements with Reddit to license data from the users on the platform. Earlier in 2025, researchers from the University of Zurich were implicated in an experiment on the same subreddit OpenAI used to train a model. They wanted to test whether an interaction with a bot was more likely to make people change their minds than an interaction with a real person. This was heavily frowned upon, and posts were all removed as users had no ability to consent to participating in a study. It has also been suggested that interactions observed by the researchers were just bots arguing with each other.
A preprint released in February 2025 by Liang et al found that the amount of content generated by AI rose from 2-3% in November 2022 to 24% by the end of 2023.



AI slop trough by Yahoo! News!




Environmnetal Impact
The facilities to run GenAI require a significant amount of resources. These facilities need a huge amount of electricity to power the facility (this places extreme strain on exising infrastructure and increases the grid’s carbon footprint) as well as water to cool the hardware. Currently, data centers use more electricity than many independent countries.
Some data centers are being built near poor communities, drain resources from, and add pollution to the community (see Colossus that has been built in Memphis to power the X bot, Grok for an example. Musk is not the only offender.)
While we cannot do anything about where data centers are built, we can make informed decisions about which platforms (if any), we use. We can also be careful with the number of queries we send, and how we use our queries. In April 2025, the CEO of OpenAI said that polite requests like “please” and “thank you” have cost tens of millions of dollars due to the cost of electricity.

title: Caution: AI in Bioinformatics
section: How To Decide When To Use AI
text:
How To Decide When To Use AI
If we know the risks and the true cost of what we are doing, we can make informed decisions about how we chose to incorporate new technologies into our day-to-day and working lives.
Here are some questions that we find useful to ask ourselves before opening a GPT:

Am I phrasing my prompt in a good way? Here is a guide to prompt engineering that might be useful
Can I find this information any other way?
How much time am I saving by looking this question up here vs on BioStars, for example?
Do I know enough about the topic to know whether the GPT is lying to me?
What are the consequences of testing the validity of the GPT solution? Can I potentially corrupt my data or my system? Is there a potential for me to lie to someone who trusts me enough to ask my opinion?

If a GPT is used to learn a new skill, remember how important active learning is. Seek explanations for everything the GPT tells you. Find independent sources that were produced by experts to validate your learning.
Hold on to the ability to learn and the desire to be curious.

All eleven are paired-end whole-genome shotgun libraries from one NextSeq 500 platform, one sequencing run each.






Note



The reads you will be given have been subset to two chromosomes. Every step of the pipeline is genuinely identical on a subset — the same tools, the same parameters, the same output structure — so nothing you learn here is specific to the reduced data.
We submit the run to the queue this afternoon and leave it to run overnight, which is how this work is normally done: you do not sit and watch a pipeline. Tomorrow morning the output will be waiting, and that is what we spend the morning on.








NoteSample names: a real-world detail worth noticing



Look at the “original name” column. It contains Pöytä1 and Elimäki1, which have non-ASCII characters, and 21161, 21271 and 2-VR-1-111, which begin with a digit.
Both will cause you trouble. Non-ASCII characters in sample names break tools unpredictably and are miserable to type in a shell; identifiers starting with a digit are mangled by R, and some tools reject them outright. This is exactly the naming problem the Linux page warns about, met in the wild.
So in the samplesheet we use the BioSample accession as the sample identifier. It is stable, unique, ASCII, starts with a letter, and points at a public record anyone can look up. Keep the human-readable names in a separate metadata file, and attach them for plot labels later:
sample,name,run
SAMEA104151691,2-VR-1-111,ERR2026087
SAMEA104151857,21161,ERR2026104
SAMEA104151879,Elimaki1,ERR2026254
SAMEA104151890,Poyta1,ERR2026265








WarningMetadata you do not get



Try looking one of these samples up in the ENA browser. The BioSample record gives you the organism, the submission date and very little else — no sampling location, no population, no provenance. That information is in the paper and its supplementary material, not in the archive.
This is worth contrasting with the fungal dataset we use later in the week, which was chosen precisely because it complies so well with FAIR principles. Both datasets are public. Only one of them is genuinely reusable without reading the paper first.
When you deposit your own data, you decide which of these two experiences you give the next person.



The reference genome
We map against GCA_965285875.1 (dhBetPend1.hap1.1), a chromosome-level assembly produced by the Wellcome Sanger Institute’s Tree of Life programme and released in 2025:







Assembly level
Chromosome — all 14 chromosomes assembled


Chromosome names
1 to 14, with INSDC accessions OZ260445.1–OZ260458.1


Chromosome sizes
18.1 Mb (chr 14) to 42.0 Mb (chr 1)


Scaffold N50
28.9 Mb


Total length
403 Mb, in 22 scaffolds, plus mitochondrion and chloroplast


Sequencing depth
about 50× long reads









NoteWhy not the assembly from the paper?





The assembly published alongside our reads in 2017 is GCA_900184695.1 (Bpev01): 5 642 scaffolds with a scaffold N50 of about 240 kb. It was a good assembly for 2017, built from short reads.
Eight years of long-read sequencing later, we can do much better, and there is no rule that says you must use the reference the original authors used. A contiguous reference means variants can be placed on chromosomes rather than on anonymous scaffolds, repeats are resolved rather than collapsed, and windowed statistics — Tajima’s D in sliding windows, Fst along a chromosome — actually mean something, because a window can follow a chromosome instead of running off the end of a 240 kb scaffold.
Reusing public reads against a better reference than the original study had is one of the quietly valuable things that open data makes possible.



Two further details matter, and both are about what a reference genome actually is.
First, dhBetPend1 is one individual tree, collected in Surrey in the United Kingdom in 2022. Our eleven resequenced trees are Finnish. The reference is therefore not a neutral backdrop: it is one tree from a different part of the species’ range, roughly two thousand kilometres from the samples we are mapping onto it. We return to what that does to the results tomorrow morning.
Second, this is hap1 of a haplotype-resolved pair — birch is diploid, the assembly separates the two haplotypes of the reference individual, and we use one of them. hap2 exists as a separate accession. So the reference represents a single haplotype of a single tree from a single meadow in Surrey.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
section: A human pipeline on a non-model organism
text:
A human pipeline on a non-model organism
This is the part of the afternoon worth paying attention to, and it is the reason we are running Sarek rather than something simpler.






Tip



There is another pipeline under development that looks like a promising alternative to nf-core Sarek for non-human and non-model species. It lives here: https://github.com/NBISweden/biovat


Sarek is excellent software, but it was written for human clinical genomics and it assumes the world that comes with that: a finished reference genome, decades of curated variant databases, and a patient. A wild birch tree is none of those things. Nothing here stops the pipeline from running, but each assumption has to be recognised and dealt with deliberately — and if you work on wild organisms, you will do this with every pipeline you ever pick up.








What Sarek assumes
How it holds for silver birch
What we do about it




The reference is one of the standard human builds, shipped via iGenomes
There is no iGenomes entry for birch
--genome null --igenomes_ignore --fasta <our reference>


A curated set of known variant sites exists (dbSNP, Mills) for base quality recalibration
No such set exists for birch. Recalibration would be trained on our own candidate variants, which is circular
--skip_tools baserecalibrator


The assembly is chromosome-level, and a sensible WGS intervals file exists
Half holds. Our reference is chromosome-level, so the scatter is over a few large intervals rather than thousands of scaffolds — but only because we chose a 2025 assembly instead of the 2017 one, which had 5 642 scaffolds. There is still no human-style WGS intervals BED, so Sarek derives intervals from the reference index
Nothing required here. Were the assembly fragmented, you would group intervals with --nucleotides_per_second or disable the scatter with --no_intervals


The organism is diploid
This one holds. B. pendula is diploid, 2n = 2x = 28
Nothing to do. Enjoy it — see the note below


Variants can be annotated against a species cache (VEP, snpEff)
No cache exists for birch
Skip annotation; when we want gene context we intersect regions of interest with a GFF3 by hand


Samples belong to patients, who have a sex and a tumour/normal status
A tree is not a patient, and birch is monoecious — individual trees carry both male and female catkins, so sex has no meaning here at all
Map each tree onto patient and sample, set sex to NA and status to 0









Important



Notice what the pattern is. Every one of these is a case where a default encodes an assumption, and where accepting the default silently would produce output that looks perfectly normal — plausible file sizes, no error messages — but is not meaningful. Base quality recalibration against your own candidate variants does not crash. It just quietly makes your data worse.
This is the central skill of the course: knowing what a tool assumes, and checking whether your organism satisfies it.








NotePloidy, and why you got off lightly



The germline callers in Sarek assume a diploid genome, and Sarek does not expose a ploidy parameter for them. For silver birch that assumption is correct, so the default does the right thing and there is nothing to configure.
Notice that this is luck, not design. Later in the week we work with a fungus that is haploid for most of its life cycle, and there the same default would produce diploid genotype calls for an organism with one copy of each chromosome — which is why the VCFtools build used for that dataset is a haploid-aware version.
Same pipeline, same default, right answer for one organism and wrong for the other. The default did not change; the organism did. Keep a note of where in a pipeline the ploidy assumption lives, because it is rarely advertised.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
text:
Before you start
From this morning you should have:

A working login to Kebnekaise
Your project ID
A directory of your own in the course project storage under /proj/nobackup/<course-project>/analysis/<group-name>







Note



You will run this in your groups. There is no need to run it both of you since it produces the same result.


Work in the project storage, not in your home directory. Nextflow writes an intermediate work/ directory that grows quickly — tens of gigabytes is normal — and a home quota will stop the run dead.






Important



Tomorrow when we have the output it is a good idea to remove the work/ directory we will not need it’s content anymore and it is good practice to free up space.


cd proj/nobackup/<course-project>/analysis/<group-name>
mkdir -p sarek_run && cd sarek_run
Set two environment variables before you launch anything. The first keeps the Nextflow Java process from claiming too much memory on the login node; the second makes containers be downloaded once into a shared cache instead of once per run.
export NXF_OPTS='-Xms1g -Xmx4g'
export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR=/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/singularity_cache






Tip



Put both lines in your ~/.bashrc so you do not have to remember them. If you forget the cache variable, every run re-downloads several gigabytes of container images, which is slow for you and unkind to everybody else on the system.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
text:
Step 1: Nextflow and containers
Find and load Nextflow:
module spider Nextflow
module load Nextflow/<version>
nextflow -version
Sarek runs each tool inside a container, so you also need a container runtime. On an HPC system that is Singularity or Apptainer, never Docker — Docker needs root privileges, which no shared cluster will give you.
module spider Singularity
singularity --version






Note



If Singularity is available without loading a module, that is normal on many systems. The check is simply that singularity --version answers.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
text:
Step 2: the smoke test
Before involving our data, run the test profile that ships with the pipeline. It downloads a tiny dataset and runs the whole workflow on it. If this works, Nextflow, the containers and the filesystem are all fine, and any later failure is about our configuration rather than the machinery.
nextflow run nf-core/sarek -r 3.12.0 -profile test,singularity --outdir test_results






Note



-r 3.12.0 pins the pipeline to one release. Without it you get whatever the default branch happens to be on the day you run, which is the opposite of reproducible. 3.12.0 is the current release as this is written — check the releases page for a newer one, but if you do change version, change it everywhere and rerun the test, because parameters occasionally move between releases.


The first time, this also downloads the pipeline itself and its containers, so it will spend several minutes apparently doing nothing. Then you should see a process list that fills in as work completes:
[85/6b7739] NFCORE_SAREK:SAREK:PREPARE_GENOME:BWAMEM1_INDEX (genome.fasta) [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
[22/cf54a8] NFCORE_SAREK:SAREK:PREPARE_GENOME:GATK4_CREATESEQUENCEDICTIONARY [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
...
Read that line. [85/6b7739] is the start of the hash of the directory where the task ran — you will need it in a moment. The name tells you which workflow, subworkflow and process it belongs to. 1 of 1 ✔ is how many tasks of that process have finished.






Tip



With default parameters the test profile runs preprocessing and calls variants with Strelka. It is small, but it is not instant. While it runs, carry on with Step 3 in a second terminal rather than watching the progress bar.








NoteIf the test fails





Work through this in order — it is almost always one of these:

nextflow: command not found — the module is not loaded in this shell.
Java heap errors — NXF_OPTS is not set.
Container pull errors or “no space left on device” — the cache variable is not set, or your quota is full. Check where you are with pwd; you should not be in /home.
Jobs fail immediately with a permission error — you are probably trying to use Docker. Use -profile test,singularity.

If none of these is it, read Step 3 and then ask us.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
text:
Step 3: what Nextflow leaves behind
This is the part of the session with the longest shelf life. Every Nextflow pipeline you ever run will fail at some point, and the debugging procedure is always the same.
Each task runs in its own directory under work/, named by that hash you saw in the console. Go into one:
cd work/85/6b7739*     # tab-completion is your friend here
ls -a
You will find:







File
What it is




.command.sh
The actual command that was run. Human-readable. Start here.


.command.log
Everything the tool printed


.command.err
Standard error — the error message lives here


.command.run
The wrapper Nextflow built, including the container and SLURM settings


.exitcode
The exit status. 0 means success.



The method for any failed process: Nextflow prints the work directory of the failure, you cd into it, read .command.err, and if that is not enough, run bash .command.sh by hand and watch it break. There is no magic in a pipeline — it is a shell command in a directory.
After the run, look at the reports Nextflow wrote:
ls test_results/pipeline_info/
The execution report tells you how long each process took and how much memory it actually used, which is how you make sensible resource requests for the real run.






Important



If a run stops and you fix the problem, relaunch with -resume (one hyphen):
nextflow run nf-core/sarek -r 3.12.0 -profile test,singularity --outdir test_results -resume
Nextflow then reuses every task whose inputs have not changed and continues from the failure. Without -resume you start from the beginning, which on real data can cost you a day. Note that it matches on file content, not just filenames, and that it only works if you relaunch from the same directory, with the same work/.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
section: Step 4: making it use the cluster
text:
Step 4: making it use the cluster
So far every task has run wherever you launched Nextflow. That is fine for a test dataset and completely wrong for real data — it would mean running an alignment on the login node.
What we want is for Nextflow itself to be a small, patient process that submits each task to SLURM as its own job. That takes a config file. Create hpc2n.config next to your run directory:
params {
    project = 'hpc2nXXXX-YYY'
}

process {
    executor       = 'slurm'
    clusterOptions = "-A ${params.project}"
    resourceLimits = [ cpus: 28, memory: 128.GB, time: 24.h ]
}

singularity {
    enabled    = true
    autoMounts = true
}
and add it with -c:
nextflow run nf-core/sarek -r 3.12.0 \
    -profile singularity \
    -c hpc2n.config \
    --input samplesheet.csv \
    --outdir results






Warning



-c is for infrastructure only — executor, resources, container settings. Do not put pipeline parameters (--input, --outdir, --tools) in a -c config file; nf-core pipelines will either ignore them or fail in a confusing way. Parameters go on the command line or in a -params-file.








NoteWhy not an institutional profile?





nf-core maintains ready-made configurations for many clusters, loaded with -profile <institution>. There is a naiss profile, but at the time of writing it only configures Arrhenius specifically, so we write our own small config for Kebnekaise instead.
The resourceLimits values above are a starting point, not a measurement. Check them against the node sizes in HPC2N’s documentation, and against what the execution report says your processes actually used.



Nextflow has to keep running for as long as the pipeline does, which can be many hours. Two ways to survive losing your connection:
# Option 1: a tmux session on the login node, detach with Ctrl-b d
tmux new -s sarek

# Option 2: let Nextflow detach itself and write to a log
nextflow run nf-core/sarek ... -bg






Tip



The Nextflow process itself uses very little CPU — it waits for SLURM — so running it on a login node inside tmux is accepted practice. It is the tasks that must go to compute nodes, and the config above is what sends them there.

title: Session 2: Nextflow Sarek setup
text:
Step 5: our own data






Important



The paths below are placeholders — the directory holding the subset reads will be given to you in the room. The accessions and the structure are real, and are what you should learn.



The samplesheet
Sarek takes a CSV with one row per sample and lane. Each of our eleven trees was sequenced in a single run, so there is one row per tree:
patient,sex,status,sample,lane,fastq_1,fastq_2
SAMEA104151691,NA,0,SAMEA104151691,ERR2026087,/proj/.../ERR2026087_1.fastq.gz,/proj/.../ERR2026087_2.fastq.gz

Column
What we put in it




patient
The BioSample accession. Sarek groups samples by patient; here each tree is its own “patient”


sex
NA. Only used for copy-number analysis in tumour/normal pairs, and meaningless for a monoecious tree

0, meaning normal. There are no tumours in a birch

The accession again

The run accession. Rows for the same sample with different lane values are merged, so using the run accession here documents where each file came from

Absolute paths to the gzipped read files



Use absolute paths. Write the remaining seven rows yourself from the table at the top of this page — it is five minutes of careful typing, and getting a samplesheet wrong is the single most common reason an nf-core run fails on the first attempt.






Tip



Check your samplesheet before you launch, not after:
# Does every file in the samplesheet actually exist?
cut -d, -f6,7 samplesheet.csv | tail -n +2 | tr ',' '\n' | xargs -n1 ls -l

# Eleven samples, eleven rows plus a header?
wc -l samplesheet.csv
Nextflow will tell you about a missing file eventually, but it is more pleasant to find out in two seconds than twenty minutes into a run.




Pointing it at the reference
Sarek defaults to human reference bundles. For birch we switch that off entirely and give it the FASTA described above:
--genome null --igenomes_ignore --fasta /proj/.../dhBetPend1_two_chromosomes.fasta
The FASTA is the only reference file that is required; Sarek builds the index, the .fai and the sequence dictionary itself. Be sure it is the assembly the reads were subset against — a reference whose sequence names do not match the reads produces an empty or nonsensical result rather than an error.


Putting it together
Rather than a very long command line, write a parameter file, params.yaml:
input: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/samplesheet.csv'
outdir: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/results'
genome: null
igenomes_ignore: true
fasta: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/reference/dhBetPend1_two_chromosomes.fasta'
tools: 'haplotypecaller'
joint_germline: true
skip_tools: 'baserecalibrator'
and launch:
nextflow run nf-core/sarek -r 3.12.0 \
    -profile singularity \
    -c hpc2n.config \
    -params-file params.yaml \
    -resume






NoteWhy those last three parameters






tools: 'haplotypecaller' — GATK HaplotypeCaller is the general-purpose germline caller. Strelka, the default in the test profile, is tuned for human data.
joint_germline: true — calls all eleven trees together and gives one multi-sample VCF instead of eleven separate ones. This is what we open tomorrow morning, and it is the only form in which the questions we care about can even be asked: allele frequencies, Fst and population structure are all comparisons between individuals, and a per-individual VCF cannot express them.
skip_tools: 'baserecalibrator' — base quality score recalibration needs a trusted set of known variants to tell real variation from sequencing error. For human data that is dbSNP. For birch no such set exists, so recalibration would be trained on our own candidate variants, which is circular. Switch it off.










Tip



Each of these is one row of the table in A human pipeline on a non-model organism. When you write the parameter file, be able to say out loud why each line is there. A parameter you copied without understanding is a result you cannot defend.

text:
Finding the output
Sarek writes its results into the directory you gave it with --outdir:
results
├── csv                 # samplesheets describing the output files
├── multiqc             # the aggregated report - start here
├── pipeline_info       # Nextflow's own execution reports
├── preprocessing       # BAM/CRAM files
├── reference           # indexes built from our reference
├── reports             # per-tool QC output
│   ├── fastqc
│   ├── mosdepth
│   ├── samtools
│   ├── bcftools
│   └── vcftools
└── variant_calling     # the VCFs
First, did it finish? Nextflow prints a summary at the end of a run, and writes the same information to the execution report:
ls results/pipeline_info/
Open the execution report in a browser. It tells you how many tasks succeeded, how many failed, how long the run took, and how much memory each process actually used.






Important



A pipeline that ends without an error message is not the same as a pipeline that did what you wanted. Check that the number of samples in the output matches the number of samples in your samplesheet. Missing samples fail quietly more often than you would like.
ls results/reports/fastqc/ | wc -l
wc -l samplesheet.csv



Opening HTML reports
The QC reports are HTML files on the cluster, and you need a browser to read them. Three ways, in order of convenience:

Start a session through Open OnDemand and open the file from the Files pane — this is what we set up on Tuesday
Open the file in VS Code with a preview extension
Copy it to your laptop with scp and open it locally

# from your laptop
scp -r <username>@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:/proj/.../results/multiqc .






Tip



MultiQC reports are self-contained single HTML files, so copying one to your laptop gives you a report that still works offline. FastQC reports are the same. This is a good format to send to a collaborator, or to attach to a thesis appendix.

title: Session 3: Quality Control and the VCF Format
text:
Part 1: FastQC
FastQC runs on the raw reads, before any trimming, and produces one report per FASTQ file — so two per sample per lane, one for R1 and one for R2.
ls results/reports/fastqc/
Open one and look at it before reading any further. Then come back.






ImportantThe single most important thing about FastQC



The green ticks, amber exclamation marks and red crosses are not verdicts on your data.
FastQC compares your file against what it expects from a random, diverse, unbiased library sequenced on a well-behaved instrument. It knows nothing about your experiment, your organism, or your library preparation. A red cross means “this is unusual for an idealised library” — which for many perfectly good datasets is simply true.
Two consequences. A red cross is an instruction to investigate, not to discard. And a column of green ticks is not evidence that your data is fit for purpose.



The modules, and what they mean for us








Module
What it shows
What to expect in our data




Basic Statistics
Read count, read length, %GC
Sanity check. Wildly different read counts between samples matter later


Per base sequence quality
Quality score by position along the read
Gradual decline toward the 3’ end is normal. A cliff is not


Per tile sequence quality
Quality by physical position on the flowcell
Localised problems — a bubble, a smudge. Usually nothing you can act on


Per sequence quality scores
Distribution of mean read quality
A second peak at low quality means a subpopulation of bad reads


Per base sequence content
%A/%C/%G/%T by position
Bias in the first ~10 bases is normal and expected (see below)


Per sequence GC content
GC distribution across reads
Watch this one. A second peak suggests another organism


Per base N content
Uncalled bases by position
Should be flat and near zero


Sequence Length Distribution
Read lengths
Uniform before trimming


Sequence Duplication Levels
How often reads are seen more than once
High duplication means low library complexity


Overrepresented sequences
Individual sequences seen often
Adapters, rRNA, or contamination. The table names what it recognises


Adapter Content
Adapter sequence by position
Rises toward the 3’ end when inserts are short. Trimming deals with it





The four worth your attention
Per base sequence quality. Quality is reported on the Phred scale, which is logarithmic:



Phred score
Probability the base is wrong
Accuracy




Q10
1 in 10
90%


Q20
1 in 100
99%


Q30
1 in 1000
99.9%


Q40
1 in 10 000
99.99%



Modern Illumina data sits around Q30–Q36 for most of the read and falls off at the end. That tail is why we trim. What should worry you is a sudden collapse, a read that starts badly, or one sample that looks quite different from the rest.
Per base sequence content. The first several bases almost always show a strong, repeatable bias. This is a well-known artefact of the random priming used in library preparation, not a problem with your sample, and FastQC flags it on nearly every genomic library ever made. What is not normal is bias continuing along the whole read, which suggests a composition problem or heavy contamination.
Per sequence GC content. This is the module to look at hardest, and the reason is biological. The DNA came from the tissue of a tree growing outdoors, and a tree is a habitat: endophytic fungi, epiphytes, bacteria and insects all live in and on it, and whatever came along in the sample was sequenced too. Because different organisms have different GC content, a contaminant shows up as a second peak or a conspicuous shoulder beside the expected unimodal distribution.
Plant material adds a second, entirely expected source of structure here: chloroplasts and mitochondria are present in many copies per cell and have their own GC content, so organellar reads can form a distinct mode of their own.






Warning



Contamination is not a hypothetical concern for field-collected plant material; it is routine. It also does not announce itself later in the pipeline: contaminant reads either fail to map, which looks like a low mapping rate, or map to repetitive and conserved regions, which looks like variants. A bimodal GC distribution now is much easier to deal with than a strange population structure plot on Thursday.


Sequence Duplication Levels. Duplicates arise when the same original DNA fragment is sequenced more than once, usually because PCR amplified it during library preparation. They matter for us because they inflate apparent read depth without adding information: ten reads that are all copies of one fragment look like tenfold coverage but carry one fragment’s worth of evidence. This is exactly why the pipeline marks duplicates before calling variants.






NoteExercise: read one report properly





Pick one sample and work through its FastQC report with a neighbour. Write down:

How many reads, and how long are they?
At which position does the mean quality drop below Q30, if it does?
Is the GC distribution unimodal? What is the modal GC content?
What fraction of reads is flagged as duplicates?
Is there adapter signal, and from which position?
Which modules got a red cross, and for each one: is it a problem, or is it FastQC being FastQC?

Question 6 is the one we will discuss as a group.

title: Session 3: Quality Control and the VCF Format
text:
Part 2: MultiQC
With eleven trees and two read files each, that is twenty-two FastQC reports, and nobody opens twenty-two of anything. MultiQC collects the output of every tool in the pipeline, for every sample, into one interactive report.
ls results/multiqc/
# multiqc_report.html   multiqc_data/   multiqc_plots/






ImportantThe single most important thing about MultiQC



Your samples are each other’s controls.
With one sample, you can only compare against a general expectation, and general expectations are weak when you work on a non-model organism. With twenty samples prepared and sequenced the same way, you have something much stronger: anything that happened to all of them is probably biology or protocol, and anything that happened to one of them is probably a problem with that one.
So do not read the report sample by sample. Read it column by column, looking for the ones that are not like the others.



How to work through the report

General Statistics, at the top, is a table with one row per sample. Click a column header to sort by it. Sort by % duplication, then % GC, then median coverage, then % mapped, and each time look at the top and bottom of the list. The same sample appearing at the bad end of several columns is your outlier.
FastQC section. The status heatmap gives you all samples by all modules at a glance. The curve plots overlay every sample, so an odd one is visible as a line that does not follow the bundle.
Alignment, from samtools stats and mosdepth: mapping rate, error rate, insert size distribution, coverage.
Variants, from bcftools stats and VCFtools: variant counts, depth distribution, transition/transversion ratio.
The toolbox on the right lets you highlight a sample in a colour across every plot in the report. Highlight your suspected outlier and scroll through — it is the fastest way to see whether one sample is consistently odd or just unlucky in one metric.







NoteExercise: find the outliers





Working in your pair, use the General Statistics table to identify the three samples you are least happy with. For each one, write a single sentence of the form:

Sample X is unusual because [metric] is [value] compared with [typical value across samples], which could be caused by [hypothesis].

Then decide, for each: keep it, keep it with a note, or drop it. Be ready to defend the decision — in particular, be ready to say what would change your mind.
This is not a trick question with a right answer. It is the actual decision that gets made in every sequencing project, usually with less discussion than it deserves.

title: Session 3: Quality Control and the VCF Format
text:
Part 3: Alignment and coverage
Here is where working on a non-model organism becomes visible in the numbers.

Mapping rate and reference bias
Our reference genome was assembled from one birch tree — and not one of ours. The reference individual, dhBetPend1, was collected in Surrey in the United Kingdom; our eleven trees are Finnish, some two thousand kilometres away. It is also a haplotype-resolved assembly, so the reference is one of that tree’s two haplotypes.
Every other tree differs from the reference, and the more an individual differs, the harder its reads are to map. Birch is wind-pollinated and outcrossing, so individuals carry a great deal of variation relative to any single reference, and a reference from the far end of the species’ range is a long way from all of our samples. For human data a mapping rate above 95% is routine, because the reference is a well-polished consensus of the species. Do not expect that here, and do not treat a lower number as failure.
What matters is the comparison across samples. A sample with a markedly lower mapping rate than the rest is telling you something: it may be more divergent, it may be contaminated, or it may not be the species you think it is.






WarningReference bias



Reads carrying the reference allele map slightly more easily than reads carrying an alternative allele, because they match the reference better. The effect is small per read and systematic across the dataset, and it pushes estimated allele frequencies toward the reference.
That matters for us specifically, because almost everything we do this week is built on allele frequencies: Tajima’s D, Fst, the site frequency spectrum, the PCA. A bias of this kind does not produce an error or an obviously wrong plot. It produces a slightly wrong answer that looks entirely reasonable.
It also does not fall equally on all samples. Trees closely related to whichever individual the reference came from are affected less than distant ones — so a bias in mapping can masquerade as a signal of population structure. Hold on to this one; it is worth raising again on Thursday when the structure plots appear.




Coverage
Mosdepth reports how deeply each part of the genome was sequenced:
ls results/reports/mosdepth/
cat results/reports/mosdepth/<sample>/*.mosdepth.summary.txt
Three things to look at:

Mean and median depth per sample. These should be broadly similar across samples. If one tree has half the depth of the others, its genotypes are less certain, and it will have more missing data after filtering. Be aware that our eleven samples were not sequenced equally: read counts in the published data range from 32.6 to 56.2 million pairs, a spread of about 1.7-fold, so some difference in depth is expected before you even start.
The cumulative coverage distribution, in MultiQC. It answers the question you actually care about: what fraction of the genome is covered at at least N× in this sample?
Coverage per contig. Our subset contains only two chromosomes, so there is not much to compare — but note what you would look at in a full dataset. The full assembly includes a mitochondrion (744 kb) and a chloroplast (161 kb), and if organellar sequences are in your reference they are covered far more deeply than the nuclear genome, because a cell contains one nucleus and many mitochondria and chloroplasts. Collapsed repeats show up as unusually deep. And a whole scaffold with conspicuously different coverage in some individuals than others is worth investigating rather than ignoring: in plants that can mean a large structural variant, and it can also mean the sample is not the species you think it is.







NoteHow much coverage is enough?





There is no single number, because it depends on what you are asking.
Calling a genotype confidently at one site in one individual needs enough reads to rule out sampling error, and in a diploid that bar is higher than you might think. A homozygote is easy: every read agrees. A heterozygote requires you to see both alleles, and each read samples one chromosome at random — so at 4× coverage there is a one-in-eight chance that all four reads come from the same chromosome and a true heterozygote is called homozygous.
That error is not random with respect to what we measure. Missing heterozygotes systematically depresses estimated heterozygosity and distorts allele frequencies, and it does so more in the samples with the lowest coverage — which is exactly why you checked whether depth varies between samples before comparing them.
But many population-genetic statistics are computed across thousands of sites and many individuals, and they tolerate uncertainty at any single site better than you might expect. This is why low-coverage sequencing of many individuals is often a better use of a budget than high-coverage sequencing of a few — you learn more about a population from 50 individuals at 5× than from 5 individuals at 50×.
What is not acceptable is coverage that varies systematically with something you intend to compare. If one group of trees was sequenced more deeply than another, then any difference you find between those groups has an alternative explanation that has nothing to do with biology. Check this now, before you do the comparison — and remember that our samples already differ by about 1.7-fold in read count.
