title: Session 3: Quality Control and the VCF Format
text:
Part 4: The VCF
Everything above was about whether to trust the data. Now we look at the data itself.
ls results/variant_calling/haplotypecaller/joint_variant_calling/






Warning



You may find two VCFs here: joint_germline.vcf.gz and joint_germline_recalibrated.vcf.gz. The second has had GATK’s variant quality score recalibration (VQSR) applied, which is a machine-learning filter trained on curated sets of known true variants.
Those training sets exist for humans. They do not exist for birch. Use the unrecalibrated joint_germline.vcf.gz, and filter it ourselves on explicit, defensible thresholds this afternoon — which is what we would have to do anyway for any non-model organism.



Looking at a VCF without regretting it
A VCF is a plain text file, usually compressed with bgzip. It is also potentially enormous. Do not open one in a text editor, and never in Excel.
VCF=results/variant_calling/haplotypecaller/joint_variant_calling/joint_germline.vcf.gz

bcftools view -h $VCF | less -S     # the header only
bcftools view -H $VCF | head -3     # the first few records, no header
bcftools query -l $VCF              # the sample names
bcftools view -H $VCF | wc -l       # how many records






Tip



less -S stops lines from wrapping, which makes a wide file readable: use the arrow keys to scroll sideways, and q to quit. Piping to head is safe even on a huge file — the pipe closes and bcftools stops.
The CHROM values in your file are whatever the sequence names in the reference FASTA are, which for our assembly means the chromosomes are named 1 to 14 — though a subset may have been renamed. Check rather than assume, with cut -f1 reference.fasta.fai or bcftools view -h $VCF | grep contig. A mismatch between what you type in a region query and what is actually in the file returns nothing at all, with no error.




Anatomy of a VCF
Every VCF has two parts: header lines beginning with ##, then one line per variant site. Here is a small, complete example:
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##FILTER=<ID=PASS,Description="All filters passed">
##contig=<ID=chr1,length=250000>
##INFO=<ID=DP,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Approximate read depth">
##INFO=<ID=AF,Number=A,Type=Float,Description="Allele Frequency">
##INFO=<ID=AC,Number=A,Type=Integer,Description="Allele count in genotypes">
##INFO=<ID=AN,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Total number of alleles">
##INFO=<ID=MQ,Number=1,Type=Float,Description="RMS Mapping Quality">
##FORMAT=<ID=GT,Number=1,Type=String,Description="Genotype">
##FORMAT=<ID=AD,Number=R,Type=Integer,Description="Allelic depths">
##FORMAT=<ID=DP,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Read depth">
##FORMAT=<ID=GQ,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Genotype Quality">
##FORMAT=<ID=PL,Number=G,Type=Integer,Description="Phred-scaled likelihoods">
#CHROM  POS ID  REF ALT QUAL    FILTER  INFO    FORMAT  SAMEA104151691  SAMEA104151857  SAMEA104151870
chr1    1420    .   A   G   982.4   PASS    DP=71;AF=0.333;AC=2;AN=6;MQ=60.00   GT:AD:DP:GQ:PL  0/0:24,0:24:72:0,72,1080    1/1:0,19:19:57:855,57,0 0/0:28,0:28:84:0,84,1260
chr1    1655    .   C   T   45.2    PASS    DP=19;AF=0.167;AC=1;AN=6;MQ=41.00   GT:AD:DP:GQ:PL  0/1:5,4:9:38:38,0,112   0/0:6,0:6:18:0,18,270   ./.:0,0:0:.:.
chr1    2310    .   G   GAT 721.9   PASS    DP=66;AF=0.500;AC=3;AN=6;MQ=59.00   GT:AD:DP:GQ:PL  1/1:0,22:22:66:990,66,0 0/0:21,0:21:63:0,63,945 1/1:0,23:23:69:1035,69,0
The header is not decoration. It is the file’s own documentation: every INFO and FORMAT field used in the records below is defined there, with its type and a description. When you meet an unfamiliar field — and you will — the definition is in the header of the file in front of you.
bcftools view -h $VCF | grep "^##INFO"
The last header line, the one with a single #, is the column header for everything that follows.


The columns








#
Column
What it holds




1
CHROM
Chromosome or scaffold name


2
POS
Position, 1-based, of the first base of REF


3
ID
Variant identifier, e.g. an rs number. . when there is none, which for us is always


4
REF
The reference allele


5
ALT
The alternative allele(s), comma-separated if more than one


6
QUAL
Phred-scaled confidence that there is a variant here at all


7
FILTER
PASS, or the names of the filters this site failed


8
INFO
Semicolon-separated annotations describing the site


9
FORMAT
Which per-sample fields follow, and in what order


10+
one per sample
The per-sample values, colon-separated, in FORMAT order



Columns 1–8 describe the site. Column 9 onwards describe the individuals. That division is the whole structure of the format, and it is worth saying out loud: everything from column 10 to the end is one individual’s data.






NoteSNPs, indels and positions





Look at the third record in the example. REF is G and ALT is GAT, which is an insertion of two bases after position 2310 — not a substitution.
This is why POS alone does not tell you how long a variant is, and why --remove-indels is one of the first things we do this afternoon. Most population-genetic statistics are defined for single nucleotide polymorphisms, and indels in a short-read alignment are considerably less reliable than substitutions.





INFO: fields that describe the site








Field
Meaning
Why you care




DP
Total read depth at the site, summed over samples
Very low depth means little evidence; very high depth often means a collapsed repeat


AF
Allele frequency of the alternative allele
The quantity most of this week is built on


AC / AN
Allele count and total alleles called
AC/AN is the frequency computed from actual calls


MQ
Root-mean-square mapping quality of the reads
Low MQ means the reads here could have come from somewhere else


QD
Quality normalised by depth
Depth-independent confidence, better for filtering than raw QUAL


FS, SOR
Strand bias measures
A real variant should appear on both strands









Tip



Extremely high DP is as suspicious as low DP. A site with five times the average depth is usually a region where two or more similar copies of a sequence have collapsed into one in the assembly, so reads from several places pile onto one location. These sites produce beautiful, confident, false variants, and they are a particular hazard in fungal genomes, which are full of repeat families and duplicated gene clusters.
This is why we will set an upper depth bound this afternoon, not just a lower one.




FORMAT: fields that describe each individual
FORMAT says GT:AD:DP:GQ:PL, so in each sample column the colon-separated values are in that order.







Field
Meaning




GT
Genotype


AD
Reads supporting each allele, reference first


DP
Read depth for this individual at this site


GQ
Phred-scaled confidence in this genotype call


PL
Phred-scaled likelihoods of each possible genotype, smallest is the call



The genotype encoding uses indices into REF and ALT: 0 is the reference allele, 1 is the first alternative, 2 the second, and so on.







GT
Meaning




0/0
Homozygous reference


0/1
Heterozygous


1/1
Homozygous alternative


./.
Missing — no call could be made


0 or 1
A haploid call, with a single allele. Not in this dataset, but you will meet these in the fungal VCF this afternoon


0\|1
Phased, with a known parental origin. We will not see these



Take the second record and read 0/1:5,4:9:38:38,0,112 out loud: heterozygous, 5 reads supporting the reference and 4 the alternative, 9 reads in total, genotype quality 38, and the likelihoods say the heterozygous call is best — but only modestly better than homozygous reference. Compare it with the first record’s 0/0:24,0:24:72:0,72,1080, where 24 of 24 reads agree. Both are calls. They are not equally trustworthy, and nothing but the numbers tells you so.






WarningHeterozygotes and allele balance



Silver birch is diploid and outcrossing, so heterozygous calls are not a warning sign here — they are most of the signal. What you check instead is whether each heterozygous call is internally consistent, and AD is how you do it.
At a true heterozygous site, each read samples one of the two chromosomes at random, so the two AD values should be roughly equal. The call 0/1:5,4:9:38:38,0,112 has 5 reads against 4, which is exactly what a real heterozygote looks like. A call like 0/1:28,3:31:20:... does not: 28 reads against 3 is not a coin flip, and something other than two alleles at one locus is generating it.
Strong allele imbalance, especially in combination with high depth, usually means one of:

Collapsed repeats or paralogues — reads from two similar regions of the genome piled onto one location, so the “alleles” are really two different loci
Contamination — a few reads from another organism or another individual
Sequencing error, particularly at low depth

The per-sample heterozygosity in the MultiQC variant section is worth a look for the same reason. A tree with far more heterozygous calls than the others may be an artefact, but in birch it may also be biology.








NoteWhy that last point is not hypothetical in birch





Silver birch, B. pendula, is diploid with 2n = 2x = 28. Downy birch, B. pubescens, grows in the same forests, resembles it closely enough that the two are regularly confused in the field — and is tetraploid. The two species also hybridise, and introgression between them is documented.
So an unusual pattern of heterozygosity in one sample is a question worth taking seriously rather than filtering away: it could be a collapsed repeat, or it could be telling you something about what that tree actually is. “Check that the sample is the species you think it is” belongs on every QC checklist for wild-collected material — and it is a check nobody can do for you after the fact.





Hands-on
VCF=results/variant_calling/haplotypecaller/joint_variant_calling/joint_germline.vcf.gz

# How many samples, and what are they called?
bcftools query -l $VCF

# How many variant records in total?
bcftools view -H $VCF | wc -l

# How many are SNPs, as opposed to indels?
bcftools view -H -v snps $VCF | wc -l

# Pull out selected fields as a table
bcftools query -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL\t%INFO/DP\n' $VCF | head

# The same, with each sample's genotype and depth
bcftools query -f '%POS[\t%SAMPLE=%GT:%DP]\n' $VCF | head

# Everything in one region
bcftools view -H $VCF chr1:1-50000 | cut -f1,2,4,5,6

# A summary of the whole file
bcftools stats $VCF | less -S






NoteExercise: interrogate the VCF






How many variants are in the file, and how many samples?
What fraction are indels rather than SNPs?
What is the median QUAL? (Hint: bcftools query, then sort -n.)
Find a site where at least one sample is ./.. Why might the call be missing there?
Find the site with the highest INFO/DP in the first 100 000 bases. Would you trust it?
For one sample, count how many genotypes are heterozygous. Then find a heterozygous call whose AD values are badly unbalanced. Would you trust it?
What does bcftools stats report for the transition/transversion ratio?

Question 7 deserves a comment. Ts/Tv is a standard sanity check: transitions are chemically easier than transversions, so real variation shows an excess of transitions, while random sequencing errors do not. In humans the expected value is well established, around 2 for whole genomes. For birch nobody has told us what to expect — so use it as a relative measure. Compute it before and after filtering, and if filtering raises it, you removed proportionally more noise than signal.

text:
Part 5: Deciding what to do about it
The point of the morning is the handover to this afternoon. Before we break, we decide together on the filtering thresholds we would apply, and why.






Important



One thing to be clear about: this afternoon we change dataset. The birch data you have just assessed is a diploid tree, sequenced whole-genome, and we looked at it to learn how to read pipeline output. For the population statistics you will work on a VCF from a forest fungus instead, with one chromosome assigned to each pair, because it is haploid, smaller, and comes with the population metadata that the statistics need.
What transfers between the two is not the numbers but the reasoning. The thresholds we agree on now are the ones you will justify, adapt and defend on a different file in an hour — which is a fair description of how this works in practice, since you will rarely assess the same dataset twice.








NoteDiscussion




Which samples, if any, are we dropping, and on what grounds? What is our rule, stated so that someone else could apply it to the same data and reach the same decision?
What minimum depth will we require for a genotype call? What maximum, and why is there a maximum at all?
What minimum quality? Raw QUAL, or QD?
How much missing data will we tolerate at a site before we discard the site? How much for an individual?
This VCF came from a diploid organism called with a diploid model, so the genotypes mean what they say. The fungal VCF we move to this afternoon comes from a haploid organism, and some of the statistics we will calculate are defined in terms of diploid genotype counts. What has to change, and what breaks if it does not?
Every filter removes real variants as well as artefacts. Which direction does each of our filters push the statistics we are about to calculate? A filter on minimum allele frequency, for instance, removes rare variants — and Tajima’s D is a statement about exactly those.
If this were your project, what would the methods paragraph say? Write three sentences.









Tip



Write the agreed thresholds down before lunch, with the reason for each next to it. You will adapt them to the fungal data this afternoon, you will want them for your report, and in a real project you will want them in six months when a reviewer asks why the numbers are what they are.

title: Containers
text:
In an ideal world I would be able to write a piece of software, or a develop some code to analyse data on my computer, and then send someone else this software or code and they could run it as well, getting the same results.
In reality, I would very likely run into at least one of the following problems:

It is not uncommon for people within the same team to use different operating systems (whether MacOS, Windows, or different flavours of Unix builds). Even if everyone is using a MacOS, there are still different versions that impact the way people are able to work with their machines.
Almost every piece of software has some sort of dependency - other software - it needs to run. Some programs might “just” need a bash shell or basic python, while others need a variety of compilers and additional libraries to function. Often, these dependencies require further dependencies to be installed. It is also not uncommon for dependencies for Program 1 to clash with the dependencies for Program 2, requiring the user to uninstall dependencies to be able to install others.
In bioinformatics, tools are very often not maintained after the student that wrote the software graduated, the PI moved to a different university, or the funding simply ran out. This leads to a lot of really good software not really being supported by newer operating systems, usually due to dependencies not being easily available or, as before, clashing with newer versions. This makes installing a tool one of the biggest hurdles to overcome in bioinformatics.
You often cannot install different versions of the same program on one computer due to conflicting names. This is particularly problematic when you want to rerun an analysis for a publication where you need to use the same software all the way through.

Any of these points might lead to you not being able to run my code, or it running but giving different results. They make bioinformatics less reproducible as tools and code cannot be moved easily betweem systems (for example if you upgrade your computer or want to share your pipeline with a colleague). Fortunately, most of these problems can be overcome with containers.

title: Containers
text:
Containers

What are containers?
Containers are stand-alone pieces of software that require a container management tool to run. They are build and exchanged as container images that specify the contents of the container, such as the operating system, all dependencies, and software in an isolated environment. The container management tool then takes the images and build the container. These management tools can be run on all operating systems, and since the container has the operating system within it, it will run the same in all environments. Container images are easily portable and immutable, so they are stable over time.


Running Containers
There are several programs that can be used to build and run containers. Docker, Appptainer, and Podman are the most commonly used platforms to date. They all have their pros and cons. If you are using a Windows machine that only you are using, then Docker is likely the least complex tool to install. On multi-user systems like a server, Apptainer is the best tool for the job. For this tutorial and the rest of the course, we will use Apptainer commands. There are small syntax changes between bash and powershell commands, but they are very similar.


Downloading Container Images
There are several repositories for people to publish container images that they have specified. Dockerhub and Seqera are two commonly used platforms for downloading container images. You are able to use container images from dockerhub on Apptainer without any problems.

dockerhub Tutorial
On the dockerhub landing page, you have a search bar, and some login options. You do not need to create an account to access the containers on dockerhub.



dockerhub landing page


For these tutorials, we’ll search VCFtools, a commonly used software for VCF manipulation and querying. The results of the search give us several different containers with the same name.



Registry search


You can see who made the container image, how many times it has been downloaded (or pulled), when it was updated (here updated means different versions of the image being uploaded), and how many people have starred it. It is usually a good rule of thumb to use the most popular images from users that have uploaded a lot of container images. The biocontainers and pegi3s profiles have builds for a lot of tools, and they are built really well!
If we click on the vcftools from biocontainers we get to a typical dockerhub image landing page:



VCFtools page


There is information on the frequency of the container image being pulled, as well as a pull command to download the image. This command is for docker, so we need to modify it for Apptainer.
apptainer pull vcftools_0.1.16-1.sif docker://biocontainers/vcftools:v0.1.16-1-deb_cv1
This command has several parts to it:

apptainer calls on the Apptainer software to run
pull tells Apptainer which function to use. In this case, we want it to go fetch something from a repository
vcftools_0.1.16-1.sif is the name of the container image on our local machine. We could call it I_Love_Dogs but that is not very informative at all. Your collaborator won’t know what it means, and you certainly won’t know what it means in 6 months from now! It is also good practice to put the version number in your image name in case you want to have several versions at the same time, and you need to tell them apart.
docker:// is the registry you are pulling from. There are several different registries, but we are only going to show 2 during this course. (You will see another one in the Seqera tutorial)
biocontainers/vcftools is the profile/repository and container you are pulling







Tip





File format extensions like .txt and .sif are really only important for us. However, it is good practice to append your files with appropriate extensions to ensure that you follow good data management practices



If you are interested in a different version than the current version, there are other versions under the tags tab:



Container versions


If you wanted to download another version of the container, you simply copy the command shown on the right side, and alter the syntax, for example
apptainer pull vcftools0.1.14.sif docker://biocontainers/vcftools:v0.1.14_cv2


Seqera Tutorial
The Seqera landing page is a bit different from the dockerhub landing page, and it works a bit differently from dockerhub. Dockerhub hosts container images that users have uploaded, while Seqera makes container images as you request them. They use bioconda, conda-forge, and pypi libraries to build their containers images with Wave. The advantage is that you can include several different softwares in your container image at once. The disadvantage is that you are limited to software hosted on the aforementioned repositories. Usually this isn’t a problem, but sometimes you want to use something that isn’t hosted there.



Seqera containers landing page


When you pull an image from Seqera and want to run it with Apptainer, you need to remember to change the container setting from Docker to Singularity, the older name of Apptainer.



Selecting Singularity


Since Seqera builds containers on-demand, sometimes you have to wait for the container to finish compiling. You can see that it is still preparing the container image from the fetching container comment. Don’t try to pull it when it is still building!



Waiting to build


When the container image is ready, you can copy the text and pull the image to your system:



Ready to download


apptainer pull vcftools_0.1.17.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/vcftools:0.1.17--b541aa8d9f9213f9
Here we use oras:// instead of docker:// as we are pulling from the oras registry. We are also pulling a different version from Seqera, so the name of the container is different.



Running Containers
Once you have the container image on your local machine, you want to be able to use it. Apptainer can be used to build the container from the image. Then you can either enter the container and run as if you had the exact same operating system as the person who built it, or you can run the software inside the container from outside of the container.
There are 2 different ways to use a container: run and exec. The apptainer run command launches the container and first runs the %runscript for the container if one is defined, and then runs your command (we will cover %runscript in the Building Containers section). The apptainer exec command will not run the %runscript even if one is defined. It is a small, fiddly detail that might be applicable if you use other people’s containers. After calling Apptainer and the run or exec commands, you can use your software as you usually would
apptainer exec vcftools_0.1.17.sif vcftools --version
This command runs your vcftools_0.1.17.sif container from the image, calls on the program vcftools that is within the container, and shows you the version. If you had installed VCFtools locally, you would have just used
vcftools --version






Important



Please remember that VCFtools is just an example. If you want to run any other tool everything after apptainer run or apptainer exec has to be substituted by the name of the specific container image and the run commands for that particular tool!




Building Containers
If the software you would like to use is not packaged into a container by anyone else, you might want to build it yourself. For this, we are just going to show a very simple example. Building containers from scratch is a computationally intensive task. You build containers from a definition file with the extension .def
Here we are going to build a container with a cow telling us the date. Save this in a file called lolcow.def.
Bootstrap: docker
From: ubuntu:20.04

%post
    apt-get -y update
    apt-get -y install cowsay lolcat fortune

%environment
    export LC_ALL=C
    export PATH=/usr/games:$PATH

%runscript
    date | cowsay | lolcat    
There are several components to this definition file.

You can set the operating system you want in the container, in this case Ubuntu 20.04.
%post section is where you update the OS from its base state, install dependencies and so on.
%environment is where you export paths and modify the environment.
%runscript is the script that will run when you use apptainer run container.sif. If you don’t include a runscript, then nothing will happen when you try to run it without any commands. You could build this container without anything in the %runscript section, and use apptainer run container.sif date | cowsay | lolcat to get the same output.

apptainer build lolcow.sif lolcow.def
You’ll get a lot of output on the status of the build, ending in
INFO:    Adding environment to container
INFO:    Adding runscript
INFO:    Creating SIF file...
INFO:    Build complete: lolcow.sif
We can now run our new container with
apptainer run lolcow.sif



Boring cow








Note



Try removing the %runscript, build it again, and see what happens.


Bootstrap: docker
From: ubuntu:20.04

%post
    apt-get -y update
    apt-get -y install cowsay lolcat fortune

%environment
    export LC_ALL=C
    export PATH=/usr/games:$PATH

%runscript
    fortune | cowsay | lolcat    
If we use the same definition file as before, but substitute date for fortune in the runscript and build the container, we now get a philosophical cow with a dark sense of humour:



Fun cow





Inspirational cow


To show the difference between the run and exec commands, we can use the same container with fortune in the runscript and run:
apptainer run lolcow.sif bash -c "date|cowsay"
and
apptainer exec lolcow.sif bash -c "date|cowsay"
The run command gives us a philosophical cow while exec gives us our boring cow again.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
text:
This afternoon we will set up BioVAT and get it running. That is the whole goal: by the time we stop at 14.30, a pipeline should be running on Kebnekaise and producing output while we go home.
We are deliberately not analysing anything today. Getting a pipeline to start — correct software, correct samplesheet, correct reference, correct cluster settings — is a real part of bioinformatics work, and it is where most of the time goes the first time you meet a new pipeline. Tomorrow morning we look at what came out of it.
BioVAT, the BIOdiversity Variant Analysis Toolkit, is a Nextflow pipeline from NBIS, built specifically for population genomics in non-model organisms. It takes raw reads and a reference genome, and gives back a multi-sample VCF together with quality reports at every stage — which is exactly the input we need for Wednesday and Thursday.






NotePlan for the afternoon




Get Nextflow and a container runtime working on Kebnekaise
Run BioVAT’s own test profile, to prove the machinery works before any of our data is involved
Look at what Nextflow left behind, so that you can debug a failure on your own
Configure BioVAT to submit jobs to SLURM instead of running them where you launched it
Point it at our data and leave it running

Steps 1–3 are the ones that matter. If you get that far and understand what you did, the afternoon was a success.


If the words Nextflow, nf-core, container and environment manager are new, the background pages on Nextflow, nf-core, Containers and Pixi cover the concepts. This page is only about making it run.

text:
What BioVAT does
BioVAT is modular: each stage can be switched on or off, and by default all of them run.








Stage
Tools
What you get




Raw read QC
FastQC
Quality metrics for the reads as they arrived


Trimming
fastp
Trimmed reads, before/after report


Alignment
bwa-mem3 (or Parabricks on GPU)

It is not an official nf-core pipeline, which mainly means you find it on GitHub rather than on the nf-core website.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
section: A pipeline built for non-model organisms
text:
A pipeline built for non-model organisms
This is the part of the afternoon worth paying attention to, and it is the reason we are running BioVAT rather than a human-genomics pipeline.
Most variant calling pipelines were written for human clinical genomics, and they assume the world that comes with it: a finished reference genome, decades of curated variant databases, a diploid organism, and a patient. Our fungus has none of these. You can run such a pipeline on a wild organism, but you spend the first day switching human-specific behaviour off, and the defaults you forget to switch off quietly damage your data.
BioVAT starts from the opposite assumption. Compare what the two kinds of pipeline expect:







Assumption in a human pipeline
How BioVAT handles it




The reference is a standard human build shipped with the pipeline
You give it any FASTA with --reference. There is no built-in genome list, so there is nothing to switch off


Known variant sites (dbSNP, Mills) exist for base quality recalibration
BQSR is not part of the pipeline at all. Even in the GATK path, BioVAT deliberately follows the Best Practices without known-variant resources


The assembly is chromosome-level
Variant calling is parallelised over genome chunks built from the reference index, grouping whole scaffolds until a chunk reaches --chunk_size. Short scaffolds can be dropped with --min_length


The organism is diploid
The caller’s ploidy is yours to set: --bcftools_call_extra '--ploidy 1'


Samples belong to patients with a sex and a tumour/normal status
Samples belong to populations, declared in a sample metadata sheet









Important



Notice what the pattern is. In a human pipeline, every one of these is a default that encodes an assumption, and accepting it silently produces output that looks perfectly normal — plausible file sizes, no error messages — but is not meaningful. Base quality recalibration trained on your own candidate variants does not crash. It just quietly makes your data worse.
Using a pipeline built for your kind of organism does not remove that problem. It moves it: now the defaults are reasonable for wild populations, and your job is to check that they are reasonable for your wild population. Below, ploidy and scaffold length are the two that matter for us.
This is the central skill of the course: knowing what a tool assumes, and checking whether your organism satisfies it.








WarningPloidy, specifically



Our organism is haploid for most of its life cycle. bcftools call assumes diploid samples unless told otherwise, so without intervention the VCF would carry diploid genotype calls for a haploid organism — mostly homozygous, since there is only one allele present, with heterozygous calls appearing where reads disagree.
BioVAT lets you pass arguments straight through to the caller, so this one is fixable:
bcftools_call_extra: '--ploidy 1'
This matters more than it looks. Several summary statistics we calculate on Wednesday are derived from genotype counts, and they are wrong if the genotypes claim two alleles where the organism has one. It is also why the VCFtools build we use later in the week is a haploid-aware version.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
text:
Before you start
From this morning you should have:

A working login to Kebnekaise
Your project ID
A directory of your own in the course project storage under /proj/nobackup/

Work in the project storage, not in your home directory. Nextflow writes an intermediate work/ directory that grows quickly — tens of gigabytes is normal — and a home quota will stop the run dead.
cd /proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>
mkdir -p biovat_run && cd biovat_run
Set two environment variables before you launch anything. The first keeps the Nextflow Java process from claiming too much memory on the login node; the second makes containers be downloaded once into a shared cache instead of once per run.
export NXF_OPTS='-Xms1g -Xmx4g'
export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR=/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/singularity_cache






Tip



Put both lines in your ~/.bashrc so you do not have to remember them. If you forget the cache variable, every run re-downloads several gigabytes of container images, which is slow for you and unkind to everybody else on the system.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
section: Step 1: getting the pipeline and Nextflow
text:
Step 1: getting the pipeline and Nextflow
BioVAT has no numbered release yet, so instead of letting Nextflow pull a version by tag, clone the repository and run it from there. You then know exactly which code you have.
git clone https://github.com/NBISweden/biovat.git
cd biovat
git log -1 --format='%H %ad' --date=short
Write that commit hash down. For a pipeline under active development it is the only honest version number you have.
Now you need Nextflow itself. There are two routes, and either is fine:
Route A — the module system on Kebnekaise
module spider Nextflow
module load Nextflow/<version>
nextflow -version
Route B — Pixi
BioVAT ships a pixi.toml that declares the exact versions of Nextflow and its helper tools the pipeline expects. If you have Pixi (see Environment managers: Pixi), you get a matching environment with one command:
pixi install
pixi run help






Tip



Route B is the more reproducible of the two, and it is a good illustration of why we cover environment managers in this course: the pipeline declares its own tooling, so you do not have to guess which Nextflow version it was tested with. pixi run help prints the pipeline’s full parameter list.


BioVAT runs each tool inside a container, so you also need a container runtime. On an HPC system that is Singularity or Apptainer, never Docker — Docker needs root privileges, which no shared cluster will give you.
module spider Singularity
singularity --version

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
text:
Step 2: the smoke test
Before involving our data, run the test profile that ships with the pipeline. It uses a small monkeyflower dataset and runs the whole workflow on it, end to end. If this works, Nextflow, the containers and the filesystem are all fine, and any later failure is about our configuration rather than the machinery.
nextflow run main.nf -profile test,singularity --outdir test_results
or, with Pixi:
pixi run test-singularity
The first time, this downloads the test data and the containers, so it will spend several minutes apparently doing nothing. Then you should see a process list that fills in as work completes:
[85/6b7739] BIOVAT:FASTQC (SAMPLE_1)        [100%] 2 of 2 ✔
[22/cf54a8] BIOVAT:FASTP (SAMPLE_1)         [100%] 2 of 2 ✔
[28/dad25a] BIOVAT:BWA_INDEX (reference)    [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
...
Read that line. [85/6b7739] is the start of the hash of the directory where the task ran — you will need it in a moment. The name tells you which workflow and process it belongs to. 2 of 2 ✔ is how many tasks of that process have finished.






Tip



The test profile limits itself to 4 cores, 15 GB and an hour, so it fits comfortably in this session. While it runs, carry on with Step 3 in a second terminal rather than watching the progress bar.








NoteIf the test fails





Work through this in order — it is almost always one of these:

nextflow: command not found — the module is not loaded in this shell, or you are outside your Pixi environment.
Java heap errors — NXF_OPTS is not set.
Container pull errors or “no space left on device” — the cache variable is not set, or your quota is full. Check where you are with pwd; you should not be in /home.
Jobs fail immediately with a permission error — you are probably trying to use Docker. Use -profile test,singularity.

If none of these is it, read Step 3 and then ask us.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
text:
Step 3: what Nextflow leaves behind
This is the part of the session with the longest shelf life. Every Nextflow pipeline you ever run will fail at some point, and the debugging procedure is always the same.
Each task runs in its own directory under work/, named by that hash you saw in the console. Go into one:
cd work/85/6b7739*     # tab-completion is your friend here
ls -a
You will find:







File
What it is




.command.sh
The actual command that was run. Human-readable. Start here.


.command.log
Everything the tool printed


.command.err
Standard error — the error message lives here


.command.run
The wrapper Nextflow built, including the container and SLURM settings


.exitcode
The exit status. 0 means success.



The method for any failed process: Nextflow prints the work directory of the failure, you cd into it, read .command.err, and if that is not enough, run bash .command.sh by hand and watch it break. There is no magic in a pipeline — it is a shell command in a directory.
After the run, look at the reports Nextflow wrote:
ls test_results/pipeline_info/
The execution report tells you how long each process took and how much memory it actually used, which is how you make sensible resource requests for the real run.






Important



If a run stops and you fix the problem, relaunch with -resume (one hyphen):
nextflow run main.nf -profile test,singularity --outdir test_results -resume
Nextflow then reuses every task whose inputs have not changed and continues from the failure. Without -resume you start from the beginning, which on real data can cost you a day. Note that it matches on file content, not just filenames, and that it only works if you relaunch from the same directory, with the same work/.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
section: Step 4: making it use the cluster
text:
Step 4: making it use the cluster
So far every task has run wherever you launched Nextflow. That is fine for a test dataset and completely wrong for real data — it would mean running an alignment on the login node.
What we want is for Nextflow itself to be a small, patient process that submits each task to SLURM as its own job. That takes a config file. Create hpc2n.config in your run directory:
params {
    project = 'hpc2nXXXX-YYY'
}

process {
    executor       = 'slurm'
    clusterOptions = "-A ${params.project}"
    resourceLimits = [ cpus: 28, memory: 128.GB, time: 24.h ]
}

singularity {
    enabled    = true
    autoMounts = true
}
and add it with -c:
nextflow run main.nf \
    -profile singularity \
    -c hpc2n.config \
    -params-file nf-params.yml \
    --outdir results






Warning



-c is for infrastructure only — executor, resources, container settings. BioVAT’s documentation is explicit that pipeline parameters must not be passed with -c; they go on the command line or in a -params-file.








NoteWhy not an institutional profile?





nf-core maintains ready-made configurations for many clusters, loaded with -profile <institution>. There is a naiss profile, but at the time of writing it only configures Arrhenius specifically, so we write our own small config for Kebnekaise instead.
The resourceLimits values above are a starting point, not a measurement. Check them against the node sizes in HPC2N’s documentation, and against what the execution report says your processes actually used.



Nextflow has to keep running for as long as the pipeline does, which can be many hours. Two ways to survive losing your connection:
# Option 1: a tmux session on the login node, detach with Ctrl-b d
tmux new -s biovat

# Option 2: let Nextflow detach itself and write to a log
nextflow run main.nf ... -bg






Tip



The Nextflow process itself uses very little CPU — it waits for SLURM — so running it on a login node inside tmux is accepted practice. It is the tasks that must go to compute nodes, and the config above is what sends them there.

title: Session 2: BioVAT Setup
text:
Step 5: our own data






Important



The raw data for the course is not finalised yet, so the paths below are placeholders. The structure is what you should learn; the exact files will be given to you in the room.



The samplesheet
BioVAT takes a CSV with one row per sequencing run. A row supplies either raw reads (fastq_1, optionally fastq_2) or an already-aligned bam/cram:
sample,library_id,flowcell_id,lane,platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,bam,single_end
Bil_01,1,AEG588A1,2,ILLUMINA,/proj/.../Bil_01_L002_R1.fastq.gz,/proj/.../Bil_01_L002_R2.fastq.gz,,
Bil_01,1,AEG588A1,3,ILLUMINA,/proj/.../Bil_01_L003_R1.fastq.gz,/proj/.../Bil_01_L003_R2.fastq.gz,,
Bnp_11,1,AEG588A2,2,ILLUMINA,/proj/.../Bnp_11_L002_R1.fastq.gz,/proj/.../Bnp_11_L002_R2.fastq.gz,,







Column
What we put in it




sample
The isolate name. Repeat it on every row belonging to that isolate — rows are merged on it


library_id
Sequencing library identifier


flowcell_id
Flowcell identifier or barcode


lane
Flowcell lane, a positive integer


platform
ILLUMINA for our data. Must be uppercase


fastq_1, fastq_2
Absolute paths to the gzipped read files


bam, single_end
Only for pre-aligned input; leave empty when giving FASTQ



Each combination of sample, library_id, flowcell_id and lane has to be unique. That is stricter than many pipelines, and it is deliberate: these four fields become the read group, which is how the pipeline can later tell a sequencing-run artefact from a biological one.






Tip



Keep the isolate naming convention from the dataset. The population prefix in the sample name is what we will group on for the rest of the week, and it is what makes the next file easy to write.




The sample metadata sheet — populations
This is the file that makes BioVAT worth using for our question. It declares which population each isolate belongs to, one row per sample:
sample,population
Bil_01,bil
Bil_02,bil
Bnp_11,bnp
Her_03,her
Passing it with --sample_metadata turns on population grouping during variant calling: bcftools call --group-samples applies the Hardy–Weinberg prior within populations but not across them. In other words, the caller stops assuming that every sample is drawn from one randomly mating pool — which for a set of isolates from Sweden, Poland, Norway, Russia and two parts of Finland is obviously false.






NoteTwo things to be careful of






Population grouping only applies with --variant_caller bcftools_multisample and the multiallelic caller (both are the defaults). With gatk the file is ignored, with a warning on the console.
Every sample in the samplesheet needs a population. Samples listed in the metadata but absent from the samplesheet are ignored, with a warning.

And a question to hold on to: if we tell the caller which population each isolate belongs to, and then on Wednesday measure differentiation between those populations, have we biased the result? Worth a few minutes of discussion when we look at the output.





The parameter file
BioVAT ships an example parameter file at assets/nf-params.yml. Copy it and edit it rather than building a long command line:
input: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/samplesheet.csv'
sample_metadata: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/sample_metadata.csv'
reference: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/reference/reference.fasta'
outdir: '/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/results'

# Workflow stages
enable_raw_read_qc: true
enable_trim: true
enable_align: true
enable_align_qc: true
enable_mark_duplicates: true
enable_variant_calling: true
enable_variant_qc: true

# Variant calling
callset_prefix: 'course_2026'
bcftools_call_extra: '--ploidy 1'
min_length: 1000






NoteThe two parameters to think about





bcftools_call_extra: '--ploidy 1' — discussed above. Our organism is haploid; the caller assumes diploid unless told.
min_length: 1000 — scaffolds shorter than this are excluded from variant calling and will not appear in the VCF. For a fragmented assembly that is usually sensible: very short scaffolds carry few variants and a lot of mapping noise. But it is a choice, and it is your choice. Set it to 0 to keep everything. The pipeline lists what it dropped in 07_variant_calls/genome_chunk_bed_files/excluded_regions.tsv and summarises it in the MultiQC report, and it warns on the console if more than 5% of the reference was excluded.
Look at that number tomorrow. “We discarded 8% of the reference before calling any variants” is the kind of thing that belongs in a methods section, and the kind of thing that is easy not to notice.





Launching
nextflow run main.nf \
    -profile singularity \
    -c hpc2n.config \
    -params-file nf-params.yml \
    -resume

title: Extra: Genome Annotation
text: It is all good and well to find signatures of selection across the genome, but if a genome is not annotated, you cannot say much more beyond “region xyz has a negative Tajima’s D”, for instance. In this course, you got a GFF3 with an annotation, but if you work with your own system, you might not have this.

title: Extra: Genome Annotation
text:
Genome Annotation
The first step is to determine where genes start and end. In this case, the reference genome has been annotated by the authors and can be found here.
If you had to perform your own annotations, you could perform an ab initio or de novo prediction using previously compiled gene prediction models from related species. There are many different tools available, and you should choose the best one for your organism. You can also create your own prediction model by sequencing the transcriptome of the organism whose genome you are sequencing. You would use a program like Augustus or GeneMark / GeneMark-ES. You will typically assemble the transcriptome (see the denovotranscript nf-core pipeline), and then use the assembly with the reference genome to train a prediction model to apply it to the assembly. You can use this hybrid appraoch through Augustus or through the Maker pipeline.

GFF3 Format
From this process, you obtain a GFF3 file. Here are is the first gene from that file

Explanation

title: Extra: Genome Annotation
text:
Functional Annotation
Once you know where the genes are, you need to know what genes do. A very comprehensive tool for this is eggNOG-mapper, and it uses orthology-based annotation rather than relying on best hits. See the prerecorded lectures on orthology.
To annotate localisation of predicted proteins, you can use DeepLoc. You might also be interested in annotating whether proteins are predicted to be effectors or not. You can annotate signal peptide regions with SignalP if you are not running DeepLoc on your predicted proteins. Proteins that have a signal peptide can be extracted and then annotated with EffectorP.

title: Extra: Genome Annotation
text:
Extracting Regions of Interest
The GFF format can be converted to BED format fairly easily by extracting columns 1, 4, and 5. By utilising this coordinate system, tools like bedtools getfasta from bedtools. If you would like to extract sequences by gene name from a multi-sequence fasta, you can use seqtk subseq from seqtk where you use a list of fasta identifiers, one per line.

title: Nextflow
text:
Amrei Binzer-Panchal.
When developing your code in bioinformatics, you will likely use different tool for different parts of your analyses. Traditionally, you would have about one script per tool, all of which you deploy by hand, one after the other. Together, this is called a workflowor pipeline.
Manual deployment of pipelines can be tedious, especially if you have analyses with many steps, or many samples of different sizes that might need a varying amount of computational power. Luckily for you, other bioinformaticians and software developers have developed something to make your life much easier:

title: Nextflow
text:
Workflow managers

Workflow managers provide a framework for the creation, execution, and monitoring of pipeline. <…> They simplify pipeline development, optimize resource usage, handle software installation and versions, and run on different compute platforms, enabling workflow portability and sharing. Wratten et al. (2021) Nature Methods

With workflow managers you can develop an automated pipeline from your scripts that can then be run on a variety of systems. Once it is developed, execute a single command to start the pipeline. The manager then coordinates the deployment of the scripts in the appropriate sequence, monitors the jobs, handles the file transfers between scripts, gathers the output, and handles re-execution of failed jobs for you. Workflow managed pipelines can run containers, which eliminates software installation and version conflicts.
That means that by design the pipelines are:

portable
more time efficient (no more downtime between pipeline steps)
more resource efficient (mostly, but this might vary depending how skilled a developer you yourself are)
easier to install (especially when combined with containers, or environment managers)
more reproducible

There are in principle two different flavors of workflow managers: snakemake, and nextflow. In this course we will be introducing you to nexflow.

title: Nextflow
text:
Nextflow
In nextflow, your scripts are turned into processes, connected by channels that contain the data - input, output etc. The order of the processes, and their interaction with each other, is specfied in the workflow scope.



source: Software carpentries








Note



In this course, we will not write our own processes, or pipeline. However, if you are interested, there are a lot of very good training materials available online.


The executable part of the processes, the so called script, can be written in any language, so in theory you could always choose the language that is best suited for the job (in practice you might be limited to the languages you know). However, the modularity of the processes allows for easy re-use of existing scripts and processes.
When moving the pipeline from one system to another, the script stays the same and does not change, the same containers are used. The only thing that changes are the parameters that pertain to the environment and available resources. In other words, with nextflow, the functional logic, the processes, are separated from the executive (how the workflow runs). This makes the nextflow pipelines highly interoperable and portable. They can be run on various platforms, such as HPC clusters, local computers, cloud systems etc..
The pipelines can be integrated with version control tools, such as git or bitbucket, and containers technologies, such as apptainer or docker. This makes the pipeline very reproducible.
The nextflow pipelines are extremely scalable, can be developed on a few samples and easily be run on hundreds or thousands of samples. When possible, processes are run in parallel automatically.
Nexflow performs automatic checks on the processes and their in- and output. It can automatically resume execution at a point of failure without having to re-compute successfully completed parts.
Nextflow is open source.

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Different operating systems bring different challenges to bioinformatics. Windows, for instance, doesn’t really support most bioinformatics tools, or your computer might run a different version of a specific tool than mine. One way to solve this, and make research more reproducible, is through the use of environments. Bioinformatics environments specify the tools neded for the task at hand, and environment managers install these tools with all their dependencies. There are many different kinds of environment managers, and for this course we are going to use Pixi.
There are, of course, other ways to solve tool access and compatibility issues, such as running virtual machines. In our experience, however, environments are a bit easier to manage and are more portable across different systems and users.



Pixi landing page


As you can see, you can run Pixi on all major operating systems, and you can include various platforms in your Pixi environment.


Installing Pixi is really easy and described thoroughly here with separate installation guides for Windows and Mac/Linux.






Tip





To source your shell, you need to source the startup files, in Linux it’s the ~/.bashrc file, in Mac it’s the ~/.zshrc file.

Pixi landing page


As you can see, you can run Pixi on all major operating systems, and you can include various platforms in your Pixi environment.


Installing Pixi is really easy and described thoroughly here with separate installation guides for Windows and Mac/Linux.






Tip





To source your shell, you need to source the startup files, in Linux it’s the ~/.bashrc file, in Mac it’s the ~/.zshrc file.

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Setting Up An Environment
You should create separate environments for each project you run, just to keep things tidy. To create an environment, you have to specify a name for your environment. You can include different platforms/operating systems in your environment, for example if you want to develop your code on a Windows system, and later use the same code on many samples on a large Linux cluster. You can also include different vetted sources for your tools, the so called channels.
Here, we will create a project called name_sida_training (please use your own name to avoid creating multiple environments with the same name). We are adding the conda-forge and bioconda channels with the -c flag.
pixi init name_sida_training -c conda-forge -c bioconda
Pixi will create a folder named name_sida_training with a a file pixi.toml. Let’s have a look at that file!






Tip





Here is the code for changing directories, listing files, and viewing the contents of a file:
cd name_sida_training
ls
less pixi.toml
To exit the less view, press q for quit.




pixi.toml
The .toml file give your information about your project. Let’s have a look at one I made one my Mac before adding any dependencies to my environment. How is it different from the one you’ve made on HPC2N?
[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
name = "sida_quarto"
platforms = ["osx-arm64"]
version = "0.1.0"

[tasks]

[dependencies]
 






Note



Your current platform will be automatically detected and added to the environment. If you want to add different platforms, you add them with the -p linux-64 flag. In this example, you are adding Linux64. See the Pixi docs for the full list of supported platforms.
If you are adding a platform that doesn’t natively run on your OS (e.g. adding Linux when running on Windows) be sure to add the OS you are running your system on as well!


Once you have used the environment, or added a dependency/tool to it, you will find yet another file, called pixi.lock.


pixi.lock
The .lock file give you information on the channels you have decided to add, as well as the information on where the packages were downloaded from, license information, md5 information, and more.






Important



Do not delete the .toml or .lock files, or you will break your environment!

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Adding Dependencies
Adding dependencies to the .toml file is telling Pixi to install the specified program for you. However, instead of installing it globally, it only gets installed in the environment.
To do this, we use the pixi add function. Let’s try adding Quarto to our environments (we will use Quarto extensively in this course!)






Important



You must be in the folder of the project to add software!


pixi add quarto






Tip





If you are unsure of how a function works, you can always query it, usually with the --help or -h flags. Here’s how it would look for the pixi add function
pixi add --help
A general rule of thumb is that a single hyphen - is followed by a single letter flag, while double hyphens -- are usually followed by multi-letter flags



Here is the pixi.toml we’ve seen earlier after I have added Quarto to my environment. You can see that the dependencies have been updated to include Quarto.
[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
name = "sida_quarto"
platforms = ["osx-arm64"]
version = "0.1.0"

[tasks]

[dependencies]
quarto = ">=1.7.32,<2"

title: Introduction to Pixi
text:
Running a Package
Now that we have an environment with a tool installed, we actually want to use it. For this we use the pixi run function.
Let’s query the help function within Quarto:
pixi run quarto --help






Note



To use other tools, simply substitute quarto with the package you’ve added, and the tool specific commands.

title: A Brief Introduction to Linux
text:
Unix-like operating systems are built under the model of free and open-source development and distribution. They often come with a graphical user interface (GUI) and can be run from the command line (CLI) or terminal. The CLI is a text-based interface that works exactly the same way as you would use your mouse, but you use words. It can be intimidating at first, but once you have mastered the basics, it’s really not different than using your mouse!
It is important to know how to use the terminal as all servers, and most bioinformatics tools do not have a GUI and rely on the use of the terminal.






Warning



MacOS and Linux, and Windows have significant differences in their syntax. Where we do things locally, we will point out some of the differences, but for the most part, we will provide Windows users with a local Linux platform so that this course can run as smoothly as possible


For this course, we do not expect you to be masters of Linux, but we will need some knowledge of how to find files, and some other basic Linux commands.

title: A Brief Introduction to Linux
text:
Filesystem Architecture
Linux uses a hierarchical filesystem, similar to Windows and Mac. In this figure from TecAdmin, there is a representation of this.



Filesystem


We can see here that the root or / folder is at the top of the hierarchy, with all other folders, like home/ and var/ inside of it.






Note





We use / at the end of a folder name to show that it is a folder.



There are two different ways for us to know where our file is within the operating system. The first is the absolute path and the second is the relative path. The absolute path gives us information that is true anywhere on your operating system. Whether your terminal is open in /usr/bin/something/ or /var/tmp/, a file will always be located at /usr/Documents/sequence.fasta as it is the true or absolute location. The relative path, as the name suggests, is relative to where you currently are on the file tree. If your terminal is open in /usr/Documents/paper/figures/linux/, the file from before, sequence.fasta will be two folders up from where you are. If you were in /var/bin/something/ it would three folder up, one to the side, and two folders down.






Tip





It is often good practice to use absolute paths when you set pipelines up to run- this way, your programs know where to go looking for the files they’re supposed to work on

title: A Brief Introduction to Linux
text:
Connecting to a Server
There are many different ways you can connect to a server with SSH. At SLUBI, we have a strong preference towards Visual Studio Code or its open-source alternative, VSCodium. It provides a graphical user interface where you can create, edit, and view files, and see the file system.
To be able to connect to a server, you need to install an extension called Remote-SSH from the extensions market place.



Extensions from View





Extensions from the shortcut


Now we need to add a host to our list of known hosts. There are several ways of doing this, and all ways lead to establishing a connection.

Under the previously shown View option, navigate to the Command Palette. A dropdown menu at the top will start with a >. Type Remote-SSH and select add new host. Here we will input our credentials. This will populate a file in a hidden folder, .ssh in your local home directories called known_hosts.
You can also write all of these lines manually. This way, you can also specify SSH keys that may be needed to log on to particular servers. We won’t be covering that in this course, though.

After a host has been added, you can connect to it. You can do this either through the Command Palette, or through the small blue backwards and forwards arrows in the bottom left corner of VSCode. You will receive a list of known hosts that you can connect to. If you need to connect with a password, a password prompt will be shown.
Once connected, you can open the file manager on the left.
For privacy concerns, we will share the exact commands locally in the room.






Important



Remeber to only open either your home directories or the folder for your projects with the file manager. If you try to open folders that are too large, you will cause VSCode to crash (and you may cause significant problems for your system administrator!)

title: A Brief Introduction to Linux
text:
Navigating with the terminal
For this part of the session, we will do some hands-on practice! For this, we will open a terminal. You can do this through the Command Palette by using the View: Toggle Terminal function, or clicking the box with a dark bottom half and an empty top half in the top right corner of VSCode.






Note





For Windows Users If you are using a Windows operating system, you can install the free Home edition of MobaXterm when your access to this server is removed if you want to continue practicing your Linux skills.
To use MobaXterm as a Linux shell, click on New Session and select a bash shell. There will probably be a prompt that you have to installl an extension. Click on the link it will provide, or copy the extension it needs and search it on Google (or your preferred search engine) and install it. Then try starting a new session again.



To see where we currently are in the filesystem, we use the present working directory command. This will give us the absolute path of the directory that our terminal open in.
pwd
To see the files that are currently in the directory we use the list command.
ls
To make a directory, we use the make directory command, followed by the name we would like our directory to have. Here we will make a directory called sida_training.
mkdir sida_training






Tip





When we give files and folders names, we don’t use spaces or special characters. It makes it really difficult to access files. We can use different ways to name our files and folders 1. youcanbechaoticandusenothing 2. YouCanUseCapitalLetters 3. you_can_use_underscores 4. you-can-use-dashes The most important thing is to be consistent with what you use, and to use descriptive names that are not too long. Future you will thank past you!



To enter the sida_training directory, we will use the change directory command.
cd sida_training
We can use the pwd command again just to make sure that we are indeed in the right folder.
To go back to the folder we were in previously, we can use a shortcut rather than the absolute path.
cd ..






Tip





There are no limits to the amount of directories you can go back (provided they are in your filesystem). If you wanted to go up 3 directories, you’d use
cd ../../..



To delete files and folder you use the remove command. If you want to remove a folder, you need a recursive flag.
rm -r sida_training
If we had a file to look at, we could use the less command. In the interface, we press q to quit.
less filename
With these Linux basics, you will certainly be able to follow our course. If you would like to learn more, Data Carpentry and Software Carpentry have excellent tutorials on using the terminal in more detail, and we can only recommend them!

title: Session 1: Introduction to Bash and HPC2N
text:
Part 1: The shell

Everyone: Software Carpentry
Work through The Unix Shell from Software Carpentry. It is the best introduction to the shell we know of, it is free, and it is written to be done on your own at your own pace.
Download the lesson data (shell-lesson-data.zip) as described in the setup instructions on the first page, and unzip it somewhere sensible in your home directory. Do not skip the data — the whole lesson is built around it.
The episodes to cover are:







Episode
Why it matters for this course




1. Introducing the Shell
Knowing what the prompt is telling you


2. Navigating Files and Directories
cd, ls, pwd — you will do this hundreds of times


3. Working with Files and Directories
Making, copying, moving and deleting your analysis folders


4. Pipes and Filters
head, wc, sort, cut, and the pipe — this is how we inspect VCFs


5. Loops
Running the same command over 20 files without typing it 20 times


6. Shell Scripts
The step before a batch script


7. Finding Things
grep and find, for when an output file has gone missing









Tip



Episodes 4, 5 and 6 are the ones that will save you the most time later in the week. If you are short on time, do those properly and skim the rest.


You are ready to move on when you can do the following without looking anything up:

Say where you are in the filesystem and list what is there, including hidden files
Make a directory, move into it, and copy a file into it using a relative path
Count how many lines of a file contain a particular word
Write a for loop that prints the name of every .txt file in a directory
Write those commands into a file and run it as a script







NoteA quick self-test





Using the Carpentry data, try to answer these with a single command line each:

How many files are in shell-lesson-data/exercise-data/animal-counts/?
How many lines does animals.csv have?
Which lines in animals.csv mention rabbits?
Write those rabbit lines to a new file called rabbits.csv.
Make a copy of every .dat file in exercise-data/alkanes/ with the extension .bak, using a loop.

If all five felt comfortable, go to the advanced track below. If they did not, stay with the Carpentry lesson — there is no advantage in rushing this.





Advanced track: OverTheWire Bandit
If you already use the shell regularly, the Carpentry lesson will be too slow for you. Instead, play Bandit.
Bandit is a wargame: each level hides a password somewhere on a server, and you need the password to log in to the next level. It teaches exactly the skills that make someone fast on a cluster — reading unfamiliar files, searching a filesystem you did not build, and dealing with awkward filenames.
Start by reading the Level 0 page, then connect:
ssh bandit0@bandit.labs.overthewire.org -p 2220
The password for level 0 is bandit0. Each level’s page lists the commands you are expected to need, and there is a link at the bottom to the next level.






Tip



Levels 0 to 10 are a good target for one morning. Levels 11 and up drift into encoding, cron and git puzzles that are fun but less relevant to us.
Keep a text file with the passwords as you go. You will want to reconnect after a break, and nobody enjoys replaying levels.








Warning



Bandit is a public server that is deliberately full of other people’s attempts. Do not put anything of your own there, and do not use a password you use elsewhere. Play it from your own laptop, not from your HPC2N account.




Advanced track, alternative: scripting drills
If puzzles are not your thing but you want something harder than Carpentry, write a small script that does something you will actually need this week.
Later in the week you will need to split the individuals in the fungal dataset into populations, because the Fst analysis takes one file of sample names per population. You can do that by hand, or you can let the sample names do the work for you: they start with a three-letter population code (Bil, Bnp, Her, Iss, …).
The sample names live on the #CHROM header line of the VCF, from the tenth column onwards:






Note



Side note: Later in the week you will be given a chromosome to extract from the main vcf, which will be the basis for your population genomics analysis. For now we only have the main vcf to work with. You can find it in the hpc2n project directory and data/phellopilus_nigrolimitatus/variation/Phenig_final_0619.recode.vcf


#!/bin/bash
# Pull the sample names out of a VCF header and write one file per population.

VCF=my_chromosome.vcf

# The #CHROM line is the last header line. Columns 1-9 describe the variant,
# everything from column 10 onwards is an individual.
grep -m 1 "^#CHROM" "$VCF" | cut -f 10- | tr '\t' '\n' > samples.txt

for pop in $(cut -c 1-3 samples.txt | sort -u)
do
    grep "^${pop}" samples.txt > "pop_${pop}.txt"
    echo -e "${pop}\t$(wc -l < pop_${pop}.txt)"
done
Run it and you get a count of individuals per population on screen, and a set of pop_*.txt files you can hand straight to vcftools --weir-fst-pop later in the week.
Then extend it:

Take the VCF as a command-line argument ($1) instead of hard-coding the filename, so it works on other vcf files too
Make it handle a compressed VCF as well (zgrep instead of grep, when the name ends in .gz)
Write the population files into a directory of their own instead of cluttering your working directory
Skip populations with fewer than four individuals, since an Fst estimate from two samples is not worth much







Note



Side note: Later in the week you will be given a chromosome to extract from the main vcf, which will be the basis for your population genomics analysis. For now we only have the main vcf to work with.








Tip



Being able to write this kind of ten-line script is worth more than knowing a hundred commands. It is also the honest answer to “how do I do this for all of my samples” — not a clever one-liner, but a loop you can read six months from now.








NoteMore things to try on your own VCF





Once you have the loop above working, these are all one or two lines each, and all of them tell you something real about the file you will be analysing for the rest of the week:

How many individuals are in your VCF?
How many header lines does it have, and how many variant lines?
Which chromosome or scaffold is yours, and what are the first and last positions in it?
How many variants are indels rather than SNPs? (Hint: compare the length of the REF and ALT fields.)
How many populations are represented, and which is the largest?

We will do all of this properly with VCFtools on Wednesday. Doing it first with grep, cut and wc is a good way to convince yourself that a VCF is just a text file, and that nothing in it is hidden from you.

title: Session 1: Introduction to Bash and HPC2N
text:
Part 2: HPC2N

What a cluster actually is
HPC2N (High Performance Computing Center North, at Umeå University) runs the cluster Kebnekaise, which is what we will use for the rest of the course. A cluster is not one big computer you log in to and work on. It has three parts that you need to keep apart in your head:

Login nodes. What you reach when you ssh in. Shared by everyone who is logged in. Meant for editing files, moving data, and submitting jobs — nothing heavy.
Compute nodes. Where the actual work happens. You never log in to these directly; you ask the scheduler for them.
A shared filesystem. Your files look the same from the login node and from every compute node, which is why a job can find your data.







Important



Never run an analysis directly on the login node. Running bwa, plink, or a Nextflow pipeline there slows the machine down for every other user on the system, and the administrators will (rightly) kill the process. Everything heavier than ls, less and a text editor goes through the batch system.


The scheduler on Kebnekaise is SLURM. You describe the job you want — how many cores, how much time, which project to charge it to — and SLURM decides when and where it runs. Your job sits in a queue until the resources you asked for are free.


Logging in
Connect from a terminal with:
ssh <your-username>@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se
You can also connect through VS Code with the Remote-SSH extension, exactly as described in A Brief Introduction to Linux, which gives you a file browser and an editor alongside the terminal.


Where to put your files
You have two places to work, and the difference matters:

Your home directory ($HOME). Small quota, backed up. Scripts, notes, configuration files.
Project storage (under /proj/nobackup/). Large, not backed up. Raw data, VCFs, Nextflow work directories, results.







Note



We will give you the exact path to the course project directory at the start of the session. In the course directory there is an analysis directory where I have made a directory for each group. If you want your own directory you can make yourself a directory with your own name in your groups directory. E.g. Say I am part of group 2 I would make this directory analysis/group_02/mimmi.








Warning



“nobackup” means exactly what it says. If you delete something there, it is gone. This is normal for HPC storage — the assumption is that raw data lives in an archive or a public repository and that everything else can be regenerated by rerunning your scripts. That assumption only holds if you keep your scripts somewhere safe.


To copy a file from your laptop to the cluster, run this from your laptop:
scp results.csv <your-username>@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:/proj/nobackup/<project_dir>/analysis/<group-name>/
For directories, or anything you might need to re-copy, rsync is better, because it only transfers what has changed:
rsync -avh my_results/ <your-username>@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:/proj/nobackup/<project_dir>/analysis/<group-name>/


Finding and loading software
Software on a cluster is not simply installed and available. There are many versions of everything, and they would conflict with each other, so instead each piece of software sits in a module that you load when you need it. This is the same idea as the Pixi environments we use elsewhere in the course — isolate what you need, declare it explicitly.
Search for software by name:
module spider R
This tells you which versions exist and, importantly, which other modules you need to load first. Kebnekaise groups software into toolchains (foss, GCC, gompi and so on), and a module is only visible once its toolchain is loaded.
Load a specific version:
module load GCC/12.3.0 R/4.3.2
See what you currently have loaded, and start from a clean slate:
module list
module purge






Tip



ml is a shorthand for module: ml R/4.3.2 and ml purge work the same way and save a lot of typing.
Always write the version number. module load R will give you whatever the default is today, and the default changes. Six months from now, “it worked in October” is not a reproducible analysis.








Important



Modules you load in your terminal are not automatically available inside a batch job. Every batch script has to load its own modules. This is the single most common reason a job dies with “command not found”.




Your first batch job
A batch script is an ordinary shell script with a block of #SBATCH lines at the top. Those lines look like comments to bash, but SLURM reads them as your resource request.
Open an editor on the cluster (vim first_job.sh is fine if you have no preference) and write:
#!/bin/bash
# Project to charge the job to - change to the course project ID
#SBATCH -A hpc2nXXXX-YYY
# A name for the job, so you can recognise it in the queue
#SBATCH -J first_job
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH -n 1
#SBATCH -c 1
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
# Where to write standard output and standard error
#SBATCH --output=first_job.%J.out
#SBATCH --error=first_job.%J.err

# Start from a clean module environment
module purge > /dev/null 2>&1

echo "This job is running on: $(hostname)"
echo "It started at: $(date)"
sleep 60
echo "It finished at: $(date)"
Submit it:
sbatch first_job.sh
SLURM replies with a job ID. Use it to follow the job:
squeue --me                  # all of your jobs, and their state
scontrol show job <jobid>    # everything SLURM knows about one job
scancel <jobid>              # stop a job
When the job is done, the output is waiting for you in first_job.<jobid>.out:
less first_job.*.out
Note which machine it says it ran on. It is not the login node.






NoteWhat the #SBATCH lines mean












Directive
What it does




-A hpc2nXXXX-YYY
The project the core hours are charged to. Jobs without a valid project are rejected.


-J name
A job name, shown in squeue. Use something you will recognise.


-N 1
The number of nodes the cores for the job can land on.


-n 1
Number of tasks (think: cores) for a serial job.


-c 8
Cores per task — this is the one you want for multithreaded tools like bwa -t 8.


--time=d-hh:mm:ss
Wall-clock limit. The job is killed when it is reached.


--output / --error
Where stdout and stderr go. %J is replaced by the job ID.


--mem
Memory, if you need more than the default per core.



Ask for what you need and not much more. Short, modest jobs start sooner than long, greedy ones, because the scheduler can fit them into gaps.





A more realistic example
The same structure, but now doing something useful: loading a module and running a tool on a file.
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -A hpc2nXXXX-YYY
#SBATCH -J bcftools_stats
#SBATCH -n 1
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=bcftools_stats.%J.out
#SBATCH --error=bcftools_stats.%J.err

module purge > /dev/null 2>&1
module load GCC/12.3.0 BCFtools/1.18

VCF=/proj/nobackup/<course-project>/<your-folder>/my_data.vcf

bcftools stats "$VCF" > my_data.stats.txt






NoteExercises






Submit first_job.sh three times in a row and look at squeue --me. What are the jobs doing?
Change --time to 00:00:30 and resubmit. What happens to the job, and where do you see the evidence?
Change the script to use 4 cores. Which directive did you use, and why?
Deliberately remove the module load line from the second script and submit it. Read the .err file. Recognising this error message will save you hours later in the week.
Use module spider to find out which version of VCFtools is available on Kebnekaise.






Interactive jobs
Sometimes you want a compute node under your fingers — to test a command, or to debug a pipeline that keeps failing. Ask for an allocation instead of submitting a script:
salloc -A hpc2nXXXX-YYY -n 1 --time=01:00:00
When the allocation is granted you can run commands on the compute node, and exit gives the resources back. Release the allocation as soon as you are finished — it is charged to the project whether you use it or not.






Tip



If you are running something long over an ssh connection, your job dies when your laptop sleeps or the network drops. tmux (or screen) on the login node solves this: start a session with tmux, detach with Ctrl-b d, and reattach later with tmux attach. For actual analyses, the real answer is to use sbatch — a batch job does not care whether you stay logged in.
